topics.summary: When to use a, an and the: I saw a dog. The dog was huge. She's a doctor. The sun is hot.
intro: ***A / an*** (the **indefinite** article) talk about one thing that isn't specific: *I need **a** pen.* ***The*** (the **definite** article) talks about something specific that the listener knows: *Can you pass me **the** pen?* (the one on the table)

Articles are difficult for many learners because some languages don't have them. This page goes step by step. For when to use **no article**, see [The or No Article](/blog/grammar/the-or-no-article/).

points.title: A or an?
points.summary: Use **a** before a consonant **sound** (*a car, a university*) and **an** before a vowel **sound** (*an apple, an hour*). Only with singular countable nouns.

blocks.md: The choice depends on the **sound**, not the letter: *an hour* (silent *h*), *a uniform* (/juː/).
Use *a / an* only with **singular countable** nouns: *a chair*. Not *a chairs* or *a water*.

examples.text: I've got **a** brother and **an** older sister.
He goes to **a** university in Toronto.

points.title: A or the? First mention and things we both know
points.summary: Use **a / an** the first time you mention something. Use **the** when it's clear which one: *I saw a cat. The cat was black.* Also **the** for things there's only one of: *the sun, the moon*.

blocks.md: ***A / an*** = one of many; the listener doesn't know which one yet: *There's **a** man at the door.*
***The*** = the listener knows which one, because:

items: we mentioned it before: *A man called. **The** man said he was your uncle.*
it's clear from the situation: *Close **the** door, please.* (the door of this room)
there's only one: ***the** sun, **the** sky, **the** internet, **the** world*.

examples.text: I bought **a** jacket and **a** shirt. **The** jacket was cheap.
There's **a** good film on TV tonight.

mistakes.wrong: I saw a film yesterday. A film was great.
mistakes.right: I saw a film yesterday. The film was great.

points.title: A / an for jobs, descriptions, prices and frequency
points.summary: Use **a / an** for jobs (*She's a nurse*), descriptions (*It's a beautiful day*), **what a…!** and to mean **per** (*twice a week, $5 a kilo*).

blocks.md: ***A / an*** is used:

items: for **jobs** and **roles**: *My father is **an** engineer.* (not *My father is engineer*)
in **descriptions** with *be*: *It's **a** great idea. She's **a** very kind person.*
in **exclamations** with a singular countable noun: ***What a** beautiful view!*
to mean ***per*** (each): *three times **a** day, 60 km **an** hour, $3 **a** kilo*.

blocks.md: With uncountable or plural nouns, *what* has no article: ***What** lovely weather! **What** nice people!*

examples.text: I go to the gym three times **a** week.

mistakes.wrong: I drink coffee two times in day.
mistakes.right: I drink coffee twice a day.

points.title: The cinema, the piano, the same, the best
points.summary: Use **the** with common places in town (*the bank, the cinema*), instruments (*play the guitar*), superlatives (*the best*), *the same, the first, the only*.

rows: *go to **the** bank / **the** post office / **the** cinema / **the** doctor's*

blocks.md: With these, *the* doesn't mean one specific building: *I'm going to **the** bank* (any branch).
Sports and games have **no article**: *play football, play chess* (not *play the football*).

examples.text: It was **the** best day of my life.
We were in **the** same class at school.

mistakes.wrong: He plays the football every weekend.
She's best student in the class.
mistakes.right: She's the best student in the class.
We go to the same school.

points.title: General statements: the tiger, a doctor, tigers; the rich
points.summary: To talk about a type in general: **plural** with no article (*Tigers are…*), **the + singular** (formal: *The tiger is…*), or **a + singular** (*A tiger can…*). **the + adjective** = a group of people (*the rich, the elderly*).

blocks.md: ***The*** + singular is also used for **inventions** and **musical instruments** in general: ***The** smartphone changed our lives.*

***The*** + adjective describes a **group of people**: *the young, the old, the elderly, the unemployed, the homeless, the blind*. It takes a **plural** verb and has no *-s*: ***The** unemployed **need** help.*

mistakes.wrong: The elephants are very intelligent animals. (in general)

points.title: Advanced article use: a coffee, a good knowledge, the French, a Mr Smith
points.summary: Articles can change uncountable nouns into countable ones (*a coffee, a knowledge of*), refer to nationalities (*the French*), and show you don't know someone (*a Mr Smith called*).

blocks.md: **Uncountable nouns with *a / an***: with an adjective or a specific type or amount: *She has **a** good **knowledge** of history. I need **a** good night's **sleep**. Two **coffees**, please.*
**Nationalities**: ***the*** + nationality adjective for the whole people: ***the** French, **the** Chinese, **the** British*. For a person: *a Frenchman / a French woman*.
**Names**: ***a*** + name = someone with that name you don't know: ***A** Mr Ahmadi called while you were out.* ***The*** + name for emphasis: *Is that **the** Taylor Swift?* (the famous one)
**Illnesses**: *a cold, a headache, a sore throat* (countable); *flu* or *the flu* (both correct); *cancer, diabetes* (no article).

examples.text: He has **a** deep **understanding** of the problem.
**The** Japanese are famous for their politeness.
**A** Ms Lopez is waiting for you in reception.

mistakes.wrong: She has good knowledge of Spanish.
mistakes.right: She has a good knowledge of Spanish.

topics.summary: Saying how often you do things: I always get up early. She's never late. We go to the gym twice a week.
intro: **Adverbs of frequency** say **how often** something happens: *always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never*.
The key thing is **word order**: they go **before** most verbs (*I **often** cook*) but **after** *be* (*I'm **often** tired*).

points.title: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never
points.summary: From most to least often: ***always*** (100%) > ***usually*** > ***often*** > ***sometimes*** > ***rarely / hardly ever*** > ***never*** (0%).

blocks.md: ***Never*** is already negative, so use a **positive** verb: *I **never** eat meat.* (not *I don't never eat meat*)
Use them with the **present simple** for habits: *I **usually** get up at 7.*

examples.text: I **always** brush my teeth before bed.

mistakes.wrong: I go always to school by bus.
mistakes.right: I always go to school by bus.

points.title: Word order: I always go, I'm always tired
points.summary: Adverbs of frequency go **before the main verb** (*I often go*) but **after** *be* (*I'm often late*) and **after** the first **auxiliary** (*I have never been, I can't always come*).

rows: *I **have never** seen it. You **can always** call me.*
***Do** you **often** go out? **Are** you **always** this busy?*
*I **don't usually** eat meat. She **isn't often** late.*

blocks.md: ***Sometimes, usually*** and ***often*** can also go at the **start** or **end**: ***Sometimes** I walk to work. I walk to work **sometimes**.*
***Always*** and ***never*** don't usually go at the start (except *Never…* for emphasis in formal English).

mistakes.wrong: We usually are at home on Sundays.
mistakes.right: We are usually at home on Sundays.

mistakes.wrong: I never have been to Paris.
mistakes.right: I have never been to Paris.

points.title: How often? Once a week, every day, twice a month
points.summary: Ask ***How often…?*** and answer with **expressions of frequency**: *every day, once a week, twice a month, three times a year, every other day*. These usually go at the **end** of the sentence.

rows: *We eat out **once a week**. She calls **twice a day**.*
*I wash my hair **every other day**.* (= every second day)
*from time to time / now and then*

blocks.md: Say ***once*** (1) and ***twice*** (2), then ***three times, four times***…: *I've been there **twice**.* (*two times* is common in speech, but *twice* is better)

examples.text: How often do you go to the dentist? ~ **Twice a year**.

mistakes.wrong: I go to the gym three times in a week.
mistakes.right: I go to the gym three times a week.

mistakes.wrong: How many often do you travel?
Every days I walk to school.
mistakes.right: Every day I walk to school.

points.title: Seldom, rarely, frequently, invariably; Rarely have I…
points.summary: More formal adverbs: ***frequently*** (often), ***occasionally*** (sometimes), ***seldom / rarely*** (not often), ***invariably*** (always, without exception). ***Rarely, seldom*** and ***never*** at the start of a sentence need **inversion**: *Rarely do we see such talent.*

rows: ***Rarely have** I seen such a beautiful view.*

blocks.md: For inversion, use **auxiliary + subject**: *Seldom **does she** complain. Never **have I** felt so happy.* See [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).
***Hardly ever*** = rarely (informal): *I **hardly ever** watch TV.*

mistakes.wrong: Rarely I have seen such a mess.
mistakes.right: Rarely have I seen such a mess.

topics.h1: And, But, Or, So and Because
topics.summary: The basic linking words: and (adding), but (contrast), or (choice), so (result) and because (reason).
intro: **Linking words** (conjunctions) join ideas: *I like tea **and** coffee. It's cheap **but** good. Tea **or** coffee? It was late, **so** I went home. I went home **because** it was late.*

This page starts with the basics and goes up to formal linkers like *however* and *therefore*. For *although* and *despite*, see [Although, Despite and In Spite Of](/blog/grammar/although-despite-in-spite-of/).

points.title: And, but, or
points.summary: ***And*** adds information. ***But*** shows a **contrast** (a different or surprising idea). ***Or*** gives a **choice**.

blocks.md: You can join **words** (*bread **and** butter*) or **sentences** (*I called her, **but** she didn't answer*).
Use ***or*** in negative sentences: *I don't like tea **or** coffee.* (not *and coffee* here)
We often put a comma before *but* when it joins two sentences: *It was sunny**, but** it was cold.*

mistakes.wrong: I like coffee but I like tea.
mistakes.right: I like coffee and I like tea.

mistakes.wrong: Do you want water and juice? (one of them)
mistakes.right: Do you want water or juice?

points.title: So or because? Result and reason
points.summary: ***Because*** gives the **reason** (why?). ***So*** gives the **result** (what happened next?): *I was hungry, **so** I ate a sandwich. I ate a sandwich **because** I was hungry.*

rows: *It was raining, **so** we stayed at home.*
*We stayed at home **because** it was raining.*
*I was tired, **so** I went to bed.*
*I went to bed **because** I was tired.*

blocks.md: ***Because*** can also start the sentence; then use a comma: ***Because** it was raining, we stayed at home.*
Don't use *so* and *because* together: *Because it was late, I went home.* (not *Because it was late, so I went home.*)

examples.text: I'm learning English **because** I want a better job.
The shop was closed, **so** I went home.
**Because** he was ill, he didn't come to work.

mistakes.wrong: Because I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.
mistakes.right: Because I was hungry, I made a sandwich.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't go out so I was ill.
mistakes.right: I didn't go out because I was ill.

points.title: Because or because of? So, that's why
points.summary: ***Because*** + a **clause** (subject + verb): *because **it was** raining*. ***Because of*** + a **noun**: *because of **the rain***. ***That's why*** = so (in speaking).

rows: *It was raining. **That's why** we stayed in.*

blocks.md: After ***because of***, use a noun, a pronoun or *-ing*: *because of **him**, because of **the traffic***.

examples.text: The flight was cancelled **because of** the snow.
The flight was cancelled **because** it was snowing.
I failed the test **because of** you!
I missed the bus. **That's why** I'm late.

mistakes.wrong: I was late because the traffic.
mistakes.right: I was late because of the traffic.

mistakes.wrong: I was late because of the traffic was bad.
mistakes.right: I was late because the traffic was bad.

points.title: Also, too, as well, either
points.summary: ***Also*** goes **before** the main verb (after *be*): *I **also** play tennis.* ***Too*** and ***as well*** go at the **end**: *I play tennis **too / as well**.* In negatives, use ***either***: *I don't like it **either**.*

rows: before the main verb, after *be* and auxiliaries
*She doesn't speak German, and I don't **either**.*

blocks.md: ***Also*** is more common in writing; ***too*** and ***as well*** are more common in speaking.
Don't use *too* in negatives: *I don't like it **either*** (not *I don't like it too*).

examples.text: He's a singer, and he's **also** an actor.

points.title: However, therefore, in addition, as a result
points.summary: In more formal writing, use linkers between sentences: ***However*** (contrast), ***Therefore / As a result*** (result), ***In addition / Moreover*** (adding). They usually start a new sentence, followed by a **comma**.

blocks.md: *But* and *so* join two parts of **one** sentence. ***However*** and ***therefore*** usually link **two sentences**: *The plan was good. **However**, it was too expensive.*
You can also put *however* in the middle, between commas: *The plan, **however**, was too expensive.* With a semicolon: *The plan was good; **however**, it was expensive.*
Don't use ***however*** like *but* with only a comma: not *It was good, however it was expensive.* Use a full stop or a semicolon.

examples.text: The hotel was lovely. **However**, the food was terrible.
Sales fell by 20%. **As a result**, 50 jobs were lost.
The job is well paid. **In addition**, it offers flexible hours.

mistakes.wrong: The weather was bad. But however, we went out.
mistakes.right: The weather was bad. However, we went out.

mistakes.wrong: It's cheap. Moreover it's bad quality. (contrast)
mistakes.right: It's cheap. However, it's bad quality.

topics.summary: Plans and predictions with evidence: I'm going to visit my aunt. Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.
intro: We use ***be going to*** + base verb for **plans** we have already decided and for **predictions** based on what we can see now: *I**'m going to** learn Spanish. Look out! You**'re going to** fall!*
To compare it with *will*, see [Will vs Going To](/blog/grammar/will-vs-going-to/). For arrangements with other people, see [Present Continuous](/blog/grammar/present-continuous/#pc-future).

points.title: I'm going to…: plans and intentions
points.summary: **am / is / are going to + base verb** for things you've already decided to do: *I'm going to buy a new phone.*

blocks.md: Use *be going to* for **intentions**: something you decided **before** speaking. *I**'m going to** clean my room this weekend.*
Common time words: *tonight, tomorrow, this weekend, next week, next year, soon.*
In fast, informal speech, *going to* often sounds like *gonna*: *I'm gonna call her.* Don't write *gonna* in formal English.

examples.text: I**'m going to** start a new job next month.
My parents **are going to** visit us in July.
He**'s going to** sell his car.
We**'re going to** watch a film tonight.

mistakes.wrong: I going to see my friends.
mistakes.right: I'm going to see my friends.

mistakes.wrong: She's going to visits her mum.
mistakes.right: She's going to visit her mum.

mistakes.wrong: They are going see a film.
mistakes.right: They are going to see a film.

points.title: Not going to and Are you going to…?
points.summary: Negative: **'m not / isn't / aren't going to**. Question: **Are you going to…? What are you going to do?**

rows: *I**'m not going to** go out tonight.*
question word + be + subject + going to + verb?
Yes, … am / is / are. No, … 'm not / isn't / aren't.

blocks.md: Put *be* before the subject in questions: ***Is** she **going to** come?* Not *She is going to come?* (in writing).

examples.text: I**'m not going to** buy that dress. It's too expensive.
**Are** you **going to** watch the match? ~ Yes, I **am**.
What **are** you **going to** wear to the wedding?
They **aren't going to** sell the house.

mistakes.wrong: What you are going to do?
mistakes.right: What are you going to do?

points.title: Predictions from evidence: It's going to rain
points.summary: Use **be going to** for a prediction based on something we can see or know **now**: *Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.*

blocks.md: When there's **evidence now** that something will happen, use *be going to*: *Look at that car! It**'s going to** crash!* *She's pregnant. She**'s going to** have a baby in June.*
The event is often very close, or we can see that it's starting: *I feel terrible. I think I**'m going to** be sick.*

For predictions based only on opinion, *will* is common: *I think she**'ll** win.* For predictions from evidence, *going to* is more natural: *She's so far ahead. She**'s going to** win.* See [Will vs Going To](/blog/grammar/will-vs-going-to/#wvg-prediction).

examples.text: Look at the sky. It**'s going to** snow.
Watch out! That glass **is going to** fall!
We're stuck in traffic. We**'re going to** be late.
The score is 4–0. They**'re going to** win.

mistakes.wrong: Look at those clouds! It rains.
mistakes.right: Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.

points.title: Going to or present continuous for plans?
points.summary: **be going to** = an intention (I've decided). **present continuous** = an arrangement (it's fixed with other people, a time and a place).

rows: *I**'m going to** see a doctor.* (I've decided to.)
*I**'m seeing** the doctor at 4.* (I have an appointment.)

blocks.md: Often both are possible: *I**'m going to** visit / I**'m visiting** my aunt on Saturday.* The present continuous suggests the plan is **fixed** (my aunt knows, we've agreed a time).
Use *going to* (not the present continuous) when it's just an **intention**, with no arrangement yet: *One day I**'m going to** climb Everest.*
With *go* and *come*, people usually prefer the present continuous to avoid *going to go*: *I**'m going** to Spain next month* (more natural than *I'm going to go to Spain*).

examples.text: I**'m going to** learn to play the guitar.
I**'m meeting** Sara for lunch on Friday.
They**'re flying** to Rome tomorrow morning.
Someday I**'m going to** write a book.

mistakes.wrong: One day I'm writing a novel.
mistakes.right: One day I'm going to write a novel.
mistakes.why: an intention without arrangements: going to

points.title: Was going to: plans that changed
points.summary: **was / were going to + base verb** = a past plan, often one that **didn't happen**: *I was going to call you, but I forgot.*

blocks.md: Use ***was / were going to*** to talk about what you **intended** to do in the past: *We **were going to** take the train, but there was a strike.*
Very often, the plan **didn't happen**, and we explain why with *but*: *I **was going to** go to the gym, **but** I was too tired.*
It can also describe a past prediction: *I knew it **was going to** rain.*
For more ways to talk about the future seen from the past, see [Future in the Past](/blog/grammar/future-in-the-past/).

examples.text: I **was going to** cook, but we ordered a pizza.
They **were going to** get married in June, but they postponed it.
Sorry, I **was going to** tell you, but I didn't have time.
I had a feeling it **was going to** be a great day.

mistakes.wrong: I was go to call you.
mistakes.right: I was going to call you.

mistakes.wrong: We are going to visit you last week.
mistakes.right: We were going to visit you last week.

points.title: Going to: imminent events, if + going to, and in formal English
points.summary: **be going to** can show something is about to happen (*I'm going to sneeze*), and **if + going to** means *if you intend to* (*If you're going to drive, don't drink*).

blocks.md: ***Going to*** is used for something that is **just about to happen** and that we often can't control: *Quick! I think I**'m going to** sneeze!*

In *if* clauses, ***going to*** is possible when it means *intend to* or when the condition is already true now: ***If you're going to** cook tonight, we need to buy some food.* (= if that's your plan)
In formal written English (reports, news, academic texts), *will* or *be expected to* is more common than *going to*: *The project **will** be completed in 2027* (rather than *is going to be*).
Compare: *If it rains, we'll stay in* (a possible future event) and *If you're going to complain all day, I'll leave* (if that's what you intend, based on how you're acting now).

examples.text: Oh no, I think I**'m going to** cry!
**If you're going to** be late, please call me.
examples.note: if you intend to / if that's the situation

examples.text: **If** we**'re going to** catch the train, we need to leave now.
The new bridge **will** open next year.

mistakes.wrong: If you will be late, call me.
mistakes.right: If you're going to be late, call me.
mistakes.why: if + going to / present (not will) for this meaning

topics.h1: Can, Could and Be Able To (Ability and Possibility)
topics.summary: Ability and possibility: I can swim. I could read at four. I'll be able to help you tomorrow.
intro: We use ***can*** for **ability** and **possibility** now: *I **can** speak three languages.* ***Could*** is the past: *I **could** swim when I was five.* For other tenses, we use ***be able to***: *I'll **be able to** help you tomorrow.*
*Can* and *could* are also used for requests and permission (*Can I…? Could you…?*). Those uses have their own page: [Requests, Offers and Permission](/blog/grammar/requests-offers-permission/).

points.title: Can and can't: ability
points.summary: **can / can't + base verb** for ability: *I **can** swim. She **can't** drive. **Can** you cook?*

rows: *I / you / he / she / we / they **can** swim.*

blocks.md: *Can* is the same for every person, with no *-s*: *He **can** sing.* Not *He cans sing*. It's followed by the base verb with no *to*: *I can **swim***, not *I can to swim*.
The full negative is written as one word: ***cannot***. In speech, *can* is usually weak /kən/ and *can't* is strong /kɑːnt/ (BrE) or /kænt/ (AmE).

points.title: Could and couldn't: ability in the past
points.summary: **could / couldn't + base verb** for general ability in the past: *I **could** swim when I was five. I **couldn't** sleep last night.*

blocks.md: ***Could*** is the past of *can* for **general ability**: *When I was young, I **could** run very fast.*
***Couldn't*** is used for both general ability and **one situation**: *I **couldn't** find my keys this morning. We **couldn't** hear the music.*
Questions: ***Could** you **swim** when you were a child?*
With verbs of the senses (*see, hear, smell, taste*) and *understand, remember*, we often use *could* for one situation: *I **could** see the sea from my window.*

examples.text: I **couldn't** open the door. It was locked.
We **could** hear the waves all night.

mistakes.wrong: When I was ten, I can swim.
mistakes.right: When I was ten, I could swim.

points.title: Be able to: other tenses and after other verbs
points.summary: Use **be able to** where *can* is impossible: *I'll **be able to** help tomorrow. I've never **been able to** dance. I'd like to **be able to** ski.*

blocks.md: *Can* has only two forms: *can* and *could*. For other tenses and structures, use ***be able to***:

rows: *I**'ll be able to** see you next week.*
*She **hasn't been able to** sleep well recently.*
*You **might be able to** get a ticket.*
*I'd love **to be able to** play the guitar.*
*I enjoy **being able to** work from home.*

blocks.md: In the present, *be able to* is possible but more formal than *can*: *Are you **able to** come?* = *Can you come?*
Don't put two modals together: *I **will be able to** come.* Not *I will can come*. *You **might be able to** help.* Not *You might can help*.

examples.text: I**'ll be able to** drive when I pass my test.
I **haven't been able to** contact him.
You **should be able to** finish by five.
I'd like **to be able to** speak French.

mistakes.wrong: I will can help you tomorrow.
mistakes.right: I will be able to help you tomorrow.
I haven't been able to finish it.
She might be able to come.

points.title: Could or was able to? Managed to
points.summary: For **one successful action** in the past, use **was able to** or **managed to**, not *could*: *The fire spread, but everyone **was able to** escape.*

blocks.md: *Could* is for **general** past ability: *I **could** swim when I was five.*

For **one particular** situation where someone succeeded (often with difficulty), use ***was / were able to*** or ***managed to***: *The road was blocked, but we **managed to** get home.* Not *we could get home*.
In the **negative**, *couldn't* is fine for both: *We **couldn't** get home.* = *We **weren't able to** / **didn't manage to** get home.*
Exception: with senses and thinking verbs, *could* is fine for one situation: *I **could** see the fire from my window.*

examples.text: She **could** play chess when she was six.
The exam was hard, but I **managed to** pass.
After two hours, firefighters **were able to** put out the fire.
I **couldn't** get a ticket. They were sold out.

mistakes.wrong: The test was difficult, but I could pass it.
mistakes.right: The test was difficult, but I managed to pass it.
mistakes.why: one success: managed to / was able to

mistakes.wrong: We managed get there on time.
mistakes.right: We managed to get there on time.

points.title: Could and can for possibility and suggestions
points.summary: **could** = something is possible (*It could rain later*) or a suggestion (*We could go to the cinema*). **can** = something is generally possible (*You can see the sea from here*).

blocks.md: ***Could*** + base verb shows that something is **possible** now or in the future, but not certain: *Take a coat. It **could** get cold later.*
***Could*** is also used for **suggestions**: *What shall we do tonight? ~ We **could** watch a film.*
***Can*** shows that something is **generally possible**: *You **can** see the CN Tower from my window. It **can** take an hour to get there in traffic.*

For future possibility, *could, might* and *may* are similar: *It **could / might / may** rain.* *Can* is not used for a particular future possibility: not *It can rain tomorrow*. See [May and Might](/blog/grammar/may-might/).

examples.text: The flight **could** be delayed because of the snow.
We **could** have a picnic if it's sunny.

mistakes.wrong: It can rain tomorrow, so take an umbrella.
mistakes.right: It could rain tomorrow, so take an umbrella.
mistakes.why: a particular future possibility: could / might

mistakes.wrong: We could to go to the beach.
mistakes.right: We could go to the beach.

points.title: Can for typical behaviour, could for criticism
points.summary: **can** = what is typical, sometimes true: *She **can** be very rude.* **could** = criticism or irritation: *You **could** at least say thank you!*

blocks.md: ***Can*** describes what is **sometimes** true or **typical** of a person, place or thing: *Scotland **can** be very wet in summer. My brother **can** be really funny.* (He isn't always funny.)

***Could*** can express **criticism** or **annoyance** about what someone doesn't do: *You **could** at least **help** me!* *They **could** have told us earlier.* (They didn't.) Stress falls on *could*.
***Could*** + *well* for a strong possibility: *Prices **could well** rise again.*
For past criticism with *could have*, see [Should Have, Could Have, Needn't Have](/blog/grammar/should-have-could-have-neednt-have/).

examples.text: The motorway **can** get very busy on Fridays.
You **could** at least **knock** before you come in!
The project **could well** take longer than planned.

mistakes.wrong: My boss can to be very strict.
mistakes.right: My boss can be very strict.

points.title: Expressions with can and could
points.summary: Common fixed phrases: *I **couldn't agree** more. I **can't help** laughing. I **can't stand** it. I **could do with** a coffee. You **can't be** serious!*

blocks.md: *Couldn't* + comparative is positive in meaning: *Things **couldn't be better*** = things are as good as possible.

examples.text: I **can't help thinking** about the accident.
This room **could do with** a coat of paint.

mistakes.wrong: I could do with to have a rest.
mistakes.right: I could do with a rest.

topics.summary: Which nouns you can count (an apple, two apples) and which you can't (water, advice, information), and how to talk about them.
intro: ***Countable*** nouns can be counted: *one apple, two apples*. ***Uncountable*** nouns can't: *water, rice, advice*. You can't say *two rices* or *an advice*.
The difference changes the words you use with them: *a, some, much, many, a few, a little*. See also [Much, Many, A Few, A Little](/blog/grammar/much-many-a-few-a-little/).

points.title: Countable or uncountable?
points.summary: **Countable** nouns have a singular and a plural (*an apple, two apples*). **Uncountable** nouns have no plural and no *a / an* (*water, rice, money*), and they take a singular verb.

blocks.md: Uncountable nouns are often **liquids** (*water, juice*), **materials** (*wood, paper, gold*), **food in a mass** (*rice, sugar, cheese*) and **ideas** (*love, help, time*).
Uncountable nouns take a **singular verb**: *The milk **is** in the fridge. Money **isn't** everything.*

examples.text: There **is** some cheese in the fridge.

mistakes.wrong: I eat a bread every morning.

points.title: Tricky uncountable nouns: advice, information, news
points.summary: Some nouns are **uncountable** in English but countable in many other languages: *advice, information, news, furniture, luggage, homework, equipment, traffic, weather, work, travel*.

rows: *a piece of news, a news story*
*a chair, a table, a piece of furniture*

blocks.md: These nouns take a **singular verb** and no *-s*: *The information **is** on the website. Your advice **was** very helpful.*
Use *some, any, much, a lot of* or *a piece of* with them: *Can I give you **some advice**? I don't have **much homework**.*

examples.text: Can you give me **some information** about the course?
I have **a lot of homework** tonight.
I'm looking for **a job**. I need **work**.

mistakes.wrong: She gave me a good advice.
mistakes.right: She gave me some good advice.

mistakes.wrong: The news are on at six.
mistakes.right: The news is on at six.

points.title: A piece of, a slice of, a bottle of
points.summary: To count uncountable nouns, use a **unit**: *a piece of cake, a slice of bread, a bottle of water, a cup of coffee, a bar of chocolate, a loaf of bread*.

blocks.md: The **unit** is countable, so it can be plural: *two **slices** of bread, three **bottles** of water*. The uncountable noun stays singular: *two slices of **bread*** (not *breads*).

examples.text: Could I have **a glass of** water, please?
She gave me **a useful piece of** advice.

points.title: Nouns that can be both: paper or a paper, coffee or a coffee
points.summary: Many nouns can be **countable or uncountable** with a different meaning: *paper* (material) / *a paper* (a newspaper); *glass* / *a glass*; *time* / *a time*; *experience* / *an experience*. With drinks, *a coffee* = a cup of coffee.

rows: *a paper*: a newspaper or an essay
*a glass*: for drinking; *glasses*: for your eyes
*hair*: all the hair on your head
*a time*: an occasion: *I've been there three times.*
*an experience*: something that happened to you
*coffee, tea, juice*: the drink in general
*a coffee*: a cup or glass of it

examples.text: I need some **paper** to print this.
I bought **a paper** at the station.
She has a lot of **experience** in marketing.

mistakes.wrong: I have a lot of experiences in sales.
mistakes.right: I have a lot of experience in sales.

mistakes.wrong: Is there a room for one more person in the car?
mistakes.right: Is there room for one more person in the car?

points.title: Formal uncountable nouns: research, evidence, feedback
points.summary: In formal and academic English, *research, evidence, feedback, knowledge, progress, accommodation, equipment* are **uncountable**. Use *a piece of*, *a study* or another countable word for one. Some uncountable nouns become countable for **kinds** (*French wines*).

rows: *a tool, a device / a program, an app*

blocks.md: These nouns take a **singular verb** and have **no plural**: *The evidence **is** clear. Recent research **has** shown…*
**Kinds**: some uncountable nouns are countable when we mean **types**: *This shop sells **French wines** and **Italian cheeses**. There are **many different teas** from China.*

examples.text: There **is** no **evidence** that the drug works.

mistakes.wrong: Recent researches show that sleep matters.
mistakes.right: Recent research shows that sleep matters.
We found a piece of evidence.

topics.summary: Which verb form comes next? I enjoy swimming. I want to swim. I'm good at swimming. I saw him swim.
intro: When one verb follows another, the second verb is often either an **-ing form** (*gerund*) or **to + base verb** (*infinitive*): *I enjoy **cooking**. I want **to cook**.* The first verb decides which form you need.

There's no simple rule for every verb, but there are useful patterns. This page goes from the basics to advanced forms. Some verbs change meaning with *-ing* or *to*: see [Verbs that Change Meaning](/blog/grammar/verbs-change-meaning-ing-infinitive/).

points.title: Like, love, hate + -ing
points.summary: After **like, love, hate, enjoy**, use **-ing**: *I like swimming. She loves reading. They hate getting up early.* (*Like / love / hate + to* is also correct.)

blocks.md: To talk about things you like or don't like doing, use ***like / love / enjoy / hate / don't mind*** + **-ing**: *I **love dancing**. My dad **hates waiting**.*

After *like, love* and *hate*, ***to*** + verb is also correct, especially in American English: *I **like to swim** / I **like swimming**.* But after ***enjoy*** and ***don't mind***, only *-ing* is possible: *I **enjoy swimming*** (not *enjoy to swim*).
**Spelling**: *swim → swimming, make → making, run → running, lie → lying*. The rules are the same as for the present continuous.

mistakes.right: She likes playing tennis. / She likes to play tennis.

points.title: Want to, need to, decide to, hope to
points.summary: After **want, need, would like, decide, hope, plan, try, learn, forget, promise**, use **to + base verb**: *I want to travel. She decided to leave.*

blocks.md: Many verbs that talk about wishes, plans and decisions take ***to*** + base verb: *I **want to** learn Spanish. We **hope to** see you soon. They **decided to** move.*
The negative is ***not to***: *I **decided not to** go.* (not *decided to not go* in careful English, though it's common in speech)

examples.text: They **plan to** get married next year.

mistakes.right: She decided to move to Spain.
I hope to see you soon.

points.title: Enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid + -ing
points.summary: After **enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid, keep, suggest, miss, practise**, use **-ing**: *Have you finished eating? I can't stop laughing.*

blocks.md: Some verbs are always followed by **-ing**, never *to*: *I **finished working** at six. He **kept talking**. Do you **mind waiting**?*
***Keep (on) -ing*** = continue or repeat: *She **keeps** **asking** me the same question.*

***Stop + -ing*** means you don't do it any more: *I **stopped smoking** last year.* *Stop + to* has a different meaning. See [Verbs that Change Meaning](/blog/grammar/verbs-change-meaning-ing-infinitive/#vcm-stop-go-on).

examples.text: Try to **avoid eating** late at night.
You need to **practise speaking** every day.

mistakes.wrong: I can't avoid to see him.
Would you mind to close the window?
mistakes.right: Would you mind closing the window?

points.title: Want someone to do: verb + object + to
points.summary: **want / would like / ask / tell / expect / help + person + to + verb**: *I want you to come. She asked me to help her.* Not *I want that you come*.

blocks.md: To talk about what you want **another person** to do, use ***want + person + to*** + verb: *I **want you to** listen. My parents **want me to** study medicine.*
Other verbs with this pattern: *would like, ask, tell, expect, help, teach, allow, advise, remind, encourage*: *She **taught me to** drive.*
***Help*** can also be followed by the base verb with no *to*: *Can you **help me (to) carry** this?*
Don't use a *that* clause after *want*: *I want **you to** come* (not *I want that you come*). See [Reporting Verbs](/blog/grammar/reporting-verbs/#rv-verb-object-to).

examples.text: My boss **expects us to** work hard.
She **asked me to** call her back.
Can you **help me move** this table?

mistakes.wrong: I want that you come with me.
mistakes.right: I want you to come with me.

mistakes.wrong: My mum wants me study more.
mistakes.right: My mum wants me to study more.
He told me to go home.

points.title: After prepositions: -ing (interested in learning, before leaving)
points.summary: After a **preposition** (*in, at, of, for, about, before, after, without*), use **-ing**: *I'm interested in learning Chinese. Think before speaking.*

blocks.md: A verb after a preposition is always in the ***-ing*** form: *She's good **at drawing**. Thank you **for coming**. **After finishing** work, I went home.*

Be careful with ***to*** when it's a **preposition**, not part of an infinitive: *I look forward **to seeing** you. I'm used **to getting** up early.* (Test: you can put a noun after it: *I look forward to the party.*)

examples.text: Are you interested **in joining** our club?

mistakes.wrong: I look forward to hear from you.
mistakes.right: I look forward to hearing from you.

mistakes.wrong: Before to leave, check the windows.

points.title: Common verbs + -ing and verbs + to
points.summary: Learn the most common patterns: **+ -ing**: *admit, avoid, consider, deny, imagine, keep, mind, miss, practise, risk, suggest*. **+ to**: *afford, agree, arrange, decide, expect, fail, hope, manage, offer, plan, promise, refuse, seem*.

blocks.md: Some verbs take **both** with little or no difference in meaning: *begin, start, continue, like, love, hate, prefer*: *It started **raining** / **to rain**.*

A useful tip: many *to* verbs look to the **future** (*hope, plan, promise, decide*); many *-ing* verbs talk about something that is **real or happening** (*enjoy, finish, avoid, admit*). It's not a perfect rule, but it helps.

examples.text: I can't **afford to buy** a car.

mistakes.wrong: I can't afford buying a new phone.
mistakes.right: I can't afford to buy a new phone.

mistakes.wrong: We considered to sell the house.

mistakes.right: She managed to finish on time.

points.title: -ing as a subject; it's worth -ing; it's no use -ing
points.summary: **-ing** can be the subject: *Swimming is good for you.* Useful phrases: **it's worth -ing, it's no use -ing, there's no point (in) -ing, have difficulty / trouble (in) -ing**.

blocks.md: An *-ing* form can be the **subject** of a sentence: ***Learning** a language **takes** time. **Smoking** is bad for you.* The verb is singular.
We can also say ***It is*** + adjective + ***to*** + verb: ***It's** hard **to learn** a language.* (more common in speech)
Fixed phrases with *-ing*:

items: ***it's worth / it isn't worth -ing***: *This museum **is worth visiting**.*
***it's no use / it's no good -ing***: ***It's no use complaining**.*
***there's no point (in) -ing***: ***There's no point waiting**. The bus has gone.*
***have difficulty / trouble / problems (in) -ing***: *I **had trouble finding** the hotel.*

examples.text: **It's** easy **to get** lost in this city.

mistakes.wrong: It's worth to visit the old town.
mistakes.right: It's worth visiting the old town.

mistakes.wrong: I had difficulty to understand him.

points.title: See someone do or see someone doing?
points.summary: After **see, hear, watch, notice, feel**: **object + base verb** = the whole action (*I saw him cross the road*). **object + -ing** = part of an action in progress (*I saw him crossing the road*).

rows: the complete action, start to finish
the action in progress (maybe not finished)

blocks.md: Use the **base verb** (no *to*) for a short or complete action: *I **heard** someone **shout**. We **watched** the plane **land**.*
Use ***-ing*** when you saw or heard the action **in progress**: *I **heard** the children **playing** in the garden.* (They were playing; I didn't hear the whole game.)
In the **passive**, *see / hear* + *to*: *He **was seen to leave** the building.* (formal)

mistakes.wrong: I saw him to cross the road.
mistakes.right: I saw him cross the road.
I heard someone knock. / I heard someone knocking.

points.title: Perfect and passive forms: having done, to have done, being done
points.summary: **having + past participle** and **to have + past participle** show an earlier action: *He denied having stolen it. She seems to have left.* **being + past participle** and **to be + past participle** are passive.

rows: perfect passive: *having been done* / *to have been done*

blocks.md: The perfect forms show that the action happened **before** the main verb. They're often optional: *He admitted **taking** / **having taken** the money.* (same meaning)
After *seem, appear, claim, pretend, be said*, the perfect infinitive is needed for a past action: *She **seems to have lost** weight.* (not *seems to lose*, which means something different)

examples.text: **Having finished** the report, she went home.
He **claims to have met** the President.
The house **appears to have been** empty for years.

mistakes.wrong: She seems to forget my name yesterday.
mistakes.right: She seems to have forgotten my name.
mistakes.why: past action: to have + past participle

mistakes.wrong: He was proud of having chose.
mistakes.right: He was proud of having been chosen.

items.prompt: I enjoy ___ to music.
My brother hates ___ the dishes.
We love ___ (go) to the beach in summer.

topics.summary: Talking about possession, family and illness with have got: I've got a brother. Has she got a car? I haven't got time.
intro: ***Have got*** means the same as ***have*** for **possession**, **family**, **appearance** and **illness**: *I**'ve got** two sisters. She**'s got** blue eyes. I**'ve got** a cold.* It's very common in **British** English, especially in speech.
In American English, people usually say *I have* and *Do you have…?* Both are correct. For *have to* (obligation), see [Must and Have To](/blog/grammar/must-have-to/).

points.title: I've got, she's got: forms
points.summary: ***I / you / we / they have got*** ('ve got). ***He / she / it has got*** ('s got). Use it for things you **own**, **family**, **appearance** and **illness**.

blocks.md: ***He's got*** = *he has got* (not *he is got*). The context tells you: *He's got a dog* (has) / *He's tired* (is).

examples.text: I**'ve got** a brother and a sister.

mistakes.right: She has got a cat. / She's got a cat.

points.title: I haven't got, have you got…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***haven't got / hasn't got***. **Questions**: ***Have you got…? Has she got…?*** Short answers: *Yes, I have. No, she hasn't.* (not *Yes, I've got*)

blocks.md: Don't use *do* with *have got*: ***Have** you got…?* (not *Do you have got…?*)

mistakes.wrong: Do you have got a car?
mistakes.right: Have you got a car? / Do you have a car?

mistakes.wrong: I don't have got a pen.
mistakes.right: I haven't got a pen. / I don't have a pen.

mistakes.wrong: Have you got a car? ~ Yes, I've got.
mistakes.right: Have you got a car? ~ Yes, I have.

points.title: Have got or have? Have breakfast, had a car
points.summary: ***Have got*** and ***have*** mean the same for **possession**. But use only ***have*** for **actions** (*have breakfast, have a shower, have a party*) and in the **past** (*I had a bike*, not *I had got a bike*).

rows: *I've got a car. / I have a car.*
*Have you got a pen? / Do you have a pen?*
*She's got a cold. / She has a cold.*
*I **had** a bike when I was a child.* (past)
*I usually **have** a shower in the morning.* (habit)

blocks.md: With ***have*** (not *have got*), questions and negatives use ***do***: ***Do** you **have** a car? I **don't have** time.*

mistakes.wrong: When I was young, I had got a dog.
mistakes.right: When I was young, I had a dog.

points.title: Have got to, got and gotten
points.summary: ***Have got to*** + verb = ***have to*** (obligation, informal): *I**'ve got to** go.* In American English, the past participle of *get* is often ***gotten*** (*It's gotten cold*), but ***have got*** (possession) is the same in both.

blocks.md: ***Have got to*** is for the **present** and **future**. For the past, use ***had to***: *I **had to** work late yesterday.* (not *I had got to*)
***Gotta*** = *(have) got to* in very informal speech and songs. Don't use it in writing.

examples.text: I**'ve got to** call my mother tonight.
We**'ve got to** be at the airport by six.

mistakes.wrong: I had got to leave early yesterday.
mistakes.right: I had to leave early yesterday.

topics.summary: Giving instructions, orders, advice and invitations: Sit down. Don't worry. Let's go. Hurry up, or we'll be late.
intro: The **imperative** is the **base form** of the verb with no subject: ***Open** the window. **Sit** down. **Don't** touch that!* We use it for **instructions**, **orders**, **advice**, **warnings** and **invitations**.
To make an imperative more polite, add ***please*** or use a question like *Could you…?* See [Requests, Offers and Permission](/blog/grammar/requests-offers-permission/).

points.title: Open the door. Don't run.
points.summary: **Positive**: base verb (*Sit down. Be quiet.*). **Negative**: ***Don't*** + base verb (*Don't worry. Don't be late.*). Use it for instructions, orders, advice and warnings.

blocks.md: The imperative is the **same** for one person or many: *Sit down, Ali. Sit down, everyone.*
With ***be***, the negative is ***Don't be***: ***Don't be** silly.* (not *Be not silly*)

points.title: Let's go, let's not, shall we?
points.summary: ***Let's*** + base verb makes a **suggestion** that includes **you and me**: ***Let's** go to the beach.* Negative: ***Let's not*** + verb (*Let's not argue*). Add ***shall we?*** to make it softer.

blocks.md: ***Let's*** = *let us*. The full form *let us* is formal: ***Let us** pray.*
***Let me*** + verb is an **offer** or a polite way to say what you're going to do: ***Let me** explain.*

examples.text: **Let me** carry that bag for you.

mistakes.wrong: Let's to go to the cinema.

points.title: Please, make sure, don't forget to
points.summary: Make imperatives friendlier with ***please***, ***just***, and phrases like ***Make sure you…***, ***Don't forget to…***, ***Remember to…***, ***Feel free to…***, ***Have a…***

blocks.md: Imperatives can sound **rude** if you say them to strangers or your boss. Use ***please***, or a question: *Could you close the door, **please**?*

mistakes.wrong: Make sure to you lock the door.
mistakes.right: Make sure you lock the door. / Make sure to lock the door.
mistakes.why: make sure + clause or to + verb

points.title: You sit here. Somebody call a doctor!
points.summary: Sometimes imperatives have a **subject** for **emphasis** or **contrast**: ***You** sit here, and **I'll** sit there.* With ***someone / everybody***: ***Somebody** call an ambulance! **Everyone** listen.* And ***Don't you dare…!*** (a strong warning).

rows: ***You** wait here. I'll get the car.*

blocks.md: A subject with an imperative can sound **impatient** or **strong**, so use it with care.

examples.text: **You** stay here. I'll be back in a minute.
**Somebody** open the window. It's too hot!

points.title: Study hard and you'll pass; hurry up, or we'll be late
points.summary: **Imperative + *and*** = *if you do this, the result will happen*: ***Study** hard **and** you'll pass.* **Imperative + *or / or else*** = *if you don't, something bad will happen*: ***Hurry** up, **or** we'll miss the train.*

rows: ***Press** this button **and** the door will open.*

blocks.md: These are common in **advice**, **warnings** and **adverts**: ***Buy** two **and** get one free!*

examples.text: **Wear** a coat, **or** you'll catch a cold.

mistakes.wrong: Hurry up, and we'll miss the bus.
mistakes.right: Hurry up, or we'll miss the bus.

items.prompt: ___ your hands before dinner.
___ late for school!
___ worry! I'll help you. (one word)

topics.summary: Using it as an empty subject or object: It's raining. It's easy to learn. I find it hard to believe.
intro: English sentences need a **subject**, so we often use ***it*** as an “empty” subject: ***It**'s raining. **It**'s five o'clock.* We also use ***it*** to **introduce** a long idea that comes later: ***It**'s important **to drink water**.* (= To drink water is important.)

This page goes from the basics to advanced patterns like *I find it hard to…* and *It goes without saying that…* For *It is said that…*, see [Passive Reporting Structures](/blog/grammar/passive-reporting-structures/).

points.title: It's raining, it's 5 o'clock, it's 10 km
points.summary: Use ***it*** as the subject for **weather**, **time**, **dates**, **days** and **distance**: ***It**'s cold. **It**'s half past six. **It**'s Monday. **It**'s 3 km to the station.*

rows: ***It**'s 5 km from here to the beach.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: ***It**'s raining* (not *Is raining*).

examples.text: How far is **it** to the airport?

points.title: It is or there is?
points.summary: ***There is / are*** says that something **exists** or is in a place (first mention): ***There's** a problem.* ***It is*** describes or identifies something **already known**: ***It's** a big problem.*

blocks.md: Use ***there*** to **introduce** something new; then use ***it*** (or *they*) to talk about it: ***There's** a new film at the cinema. **It**'s really funny.*

examples.text: **There's** a bank on the corner. **It** opens at 9.

mistakes.wrong: It's a supermarket near here. (first mention)

points.title: It's easy to learn, it's nice to meet you
points.summary: ***It's*** + **adjective** + ***to*** + verb: ***It's easy to** use. **It's nice to** meet you.* Add ***for*** + person: ***It's hard for me to** understand.* Also ***It takes*** + time + ***to***: ***It takes** an hour **to** get there.*

rows: ***It's difficult for children to** sit still.*
***It was kind of you to** help.*

blocks.md: This is more natural than starting with *to*: ***It's** easy **to** cook pasta* (not usually *To cook pasta is easy*).

mistakes.wrong: It's difficult to me to understand.
mistakes.right: It's difficult for me to understand.

points.title: It's a shame that, it seems that, it doesn't matter
points.summary: ***It*** + *be* + adjective / noun + ***that***-clause: ***It's a shame that** you can't come. **It's obvious that** he's lying.* With verbs: ***It seems / appears / turns out that…*** ***It doesn't matter whether / what…***

rows: ***It's a pity that** you missed the party.*
***It turned out that** she was right.*

blocks.md: ***That*** can often be left out in speech: ***It's a shame** you can't come.*

examples.text: **It's** a shame **that** the concert was cancelled.
**It seems that** the train is late again.
**It turned out that** we were in the wrong room.

mistakes.wrong: It's a pity what you can't come.
mistakes.right: It's a pity that you can't come.

points.title: I find it hard to, I'd appreciate it if, make it clear
points.summary: ***It*** can also be a **preparatory object**: ***I find it hard to** believe. **I'd appreciate it if** you could help. **She made it clear that** she was unhappy. **I take it** you're not coming.*

rows: ***I'd appreciate it if** you didn't smoke here.*
***I hate it when** people are late.*
***I take it** you've heard the news.*

blocks.md: Don't leave out ***it***: *I find **it** hard to sleep* (not *I find hard to sleep*). *I'd appreciate **it** if…* (not *I'd appreciate if…*).

examples.text: I **find it** easy **to** talk to her.
The teacher **made it clear that** phones weren't allowed.
**I'd appreciate it if** you could reply soon.

mistakes.wrong: I find difficult to wake up early.
mistakes.right: I find it difficult to wake up early.

mistakes.wrong: I'd appreciate if you could call me.
mistakes.right: I'd appreciate it if you could call me.

points.title: It's no use, it's worth, it goes without saying
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***It's no use / no good*** + *-ing*, ***It's worth*** + *-ing*, ***It goes without saying that…***, ***It remains to be seen whether…***, ***It stands to reason that…***, ***It's not for me to…***

rows: ***It goes without saying that** safety comes first.*
***It remains to be seen whether** the plan will work.*
***It stands to reason that** prices will rise.*

blocks.md: After ***no use / no good / worth***, use ***-ing***: *It's no use **complaining*** (not *to complain*).

examples.text: **It's no use** arguing with him. He never listens.
**It goes without saying that** you'll be paid.
**It remains to be seen whether** he'll accept the offer.

mistakes.wrong: It's no use cry about it.
mistakes.right: It's no use crying about it.

mistakes.wrong: It's worth to visit the castle.

topics.h1: Much, Many, A Lot Of, A Few, A Little
topics.summary: Talking about quantity: How much money? How many people? A lot of time, a few friends, a little sugar.
intro: Use ***many*** and ***a few*** with **plural countable** nouns (*many books, a few friends*), and ***much*** and ***a little*** with **uncountable** nouns (*much time, a little milk*). ***A lot of*** works with both.
See also [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/) and [Some and Any](/blog/grammar/some-any/).

points.title: Much, many, a lot of; how much, how many
points.summary: Use ***many*** + plural nouns and ***much*** + uncountable nouns, mostly in **questions and negatives**. Use ***a lot of / lots of*** with both, especially in **positive** sentences. Ask ***How many…?*** and ***How much…?***

blocks.md: In positive sentences, ***a lot of*** sounds more natural than *much*: *I drink **a lot of** coffee.* (not *I drink much coffee*). *Many* is fine in positive sentences, but *a lot of* is more common in speech.
***How much*** also asks about **price**: *How much is this jacket?*

examples.text: There are **a lot of** people here.

mistakes.wrong: There is a lot of cars.
mistakes.right: There are a lot of cars.

points.title: A few and a little: some, but not a lot
points.summary: ***A few*** + plural nouns and ***a little*** + uncountable nouns mean **some, a small amount**: *I have a few friends here. Can I have a little sugar?*

rows: *a few eggs, a few days, a few people*
*a little milk, a little time, a little money*

blocks.md: *A few* and *a little* are **positive**: they mean *some*, often *enough*: *I have **a few** friends in Toronto, so I'm not lonely.*
***A little*** can also mean *a bit* before an adjective: *I'm **a little** tired.*

examples.text: I'll be ready in **a few** minutes.
We stayed in Paris for **a few** days.

mistakes.wrong: I have a little friends here.
mistakes.right: I have a few friends here.

mistakes.wrong: Can I have a few milk?
mistakes.right: Can I have a little milk?

points.title: Few or a few? Little or a little?
points.summary: ***A few / a little*** = **some** (positive). ***Few / little*** (without *a*) = **not many / not much** (negative): *I have a few friends* (I'm OK). *I have few friends* (I'm lonely).

rows: *There's **a little** time left. Let's have a coffee.*

blocks.md: *Few* and *little* (without *a*) are quite **formal**. In conversation, people usually say *not many / not much*: *Not many people came.*
***Very few / very little*** are common: *There's **very little** money left.*
***Quite a few*** = quite a lot: *Quite a few people came.*

examples.text: **Few** tourists visit this area in winter.
He has **little** patience with lazy students.
**A few** of my friends came to help.

mistakes.wrong: Unfortunately, a few people came, so the party was boring.
mistakes.right: Unfortunately, few people came, so the party was boring.
Don't hurry. There's a little time.

points.title: Too much, too many, plenty of, a large number of
points.summary: ***Too much / too many*** = more than you want. ***Plenty of*** = more than enough. In formal English: ***a large number of*** + plural nouns, ***a great deal of / a large amount of*** + uncountable nouns.

rows: *a great deal of money, a large amount of data*

blocks.md: ***Plenty of*** is positive: *Don't worry, we have **plenty of** time.* (= more than enough)
In formal writing, use ***a large number of*** with countable nouns and ***a great deal of / a large amount of*** with uncountable nouns. Don't use *a great deal of* with plural nouns.

examples.text: There are **too many** cars in the city centre.
I spend **too much** time on my phone.
The project requires **a great deal of** effort.

mistakes.wrong: A large number of money was stolen.
mistakes.right: A large amount of money was stolen.

mistakes.wrong: A great deal of people agree.
mistakes.right: A large number of people agree.

points.title: Much in formal writing, many a, a great many
points.summary: In **formal** English, ***much*** and ***many*** are common in positive sentences: *Much has been written about this.* ***Many a*** + singular noun = many (literary). ***A good / great many*** = a very large number.

rows: ***Much** research has been done on this topic. There is **much** debate about…*
***Much** of the city was destroyed. **Many** believe that…*

blocks.md: In everyday speech, *a lot of* is more natural in positive sentences. In academic and formal writing, ***much*** and ***many*** are common: *There has been **much** discussion of…*
***As much as / as many as*** + number emphasises that the number is **large**: *As many as 10,000 people were affected.* Use *as much as* for money and uncountable amounts.

examples.text: **Many a** traveller has got lost in these mountains.
She has written **a great many** articles.
**As many as** 500 jobs could be lost.

mistakes.why: many a + singular noun + singular verb

mistakes.wrong: A great many people was there.
mistakes.right: A great many people were there.

mistakes.wrong: It can cost as many as $1,000.
mistakes.right: It can cost as much as $1,000.

topics.h1: Object Pronouns: Me, Him, Her, Us, Them
topics.summary: Using me, you, him, her, it, us and them after verbs and prepositions: Call me. I like her. Come with us.
intro: **Object pronouns** (*me, you, him, her, it, us, them*) come **after** a verb or a preposition: *Can you help **me**? I'm waiting for **them**.*
For *I, he, she, they*, see [Subject Pronouns and Possessive Adjectives](/blog/grammar/subject-pronouns-possessive-adjectives/).

points.title: Me, you, him, her, it, us, them after a verb
points.summary: Use an **object pronoun** after a verb: *I love **her**. She called **me**. We saw **them**.*

blocks.md: The subject does the action; the object receives it: ***She** helps **me**. **I** help **her**.*
*You* and *it* don't change.

examples.text: Where are my keys? I can't find **them**.

mistakes.wrong: I bought a new phone, but I don't like.
mistakes.right: I bought a new phone, but I don't like it.
mistakes.why: the verb needs an object: it

points.title: Object pronouns after prepositions: with me, for them
points.summary: Use **object pronouns** after **prepositions**: *with me, for her, about him, to us, from them*.

blocks.md: Prepositions (*with, for, to, about, at, from, without, near, behind*) are followed by **object** pronouns: *Come **with us**! This is **for you**. Look **at me**.*
Some verbs need a preposition before the object: *listen **to** me, wait **for** him, look **at** them, talk **to** her*.

examples.text: I often talk **to them** on the phone.

points.title: Me too, it's me, my friend and I
points.summary: In short answers and after ***be***, use **object pronouns** in everyday English: *Me too! Who's there? ~ It's me.* In a subject with **two people**, use the **subject** form, and put yourself **last**: *My friend and I went to the cinema.*

rows: *I do / I am* is also possible
*Me and my friend went out* is very informal

blocks.md: To check the pronoun, remove the other person: *My friend and **I** went out* → ***I** went out*. *She invited my friend and **me*** → *She invited **me***.
*Me and my friend went…* is common in casual speech, but it's considered incorrect in writing and exams.

examples.text: Our teacher gave **Ali and me** extra homework.

mistakes.wrong: Me and Sara are going to the cinema.
mistakes.right: Sara and I are going to the cinema.
mistakes.why: subject: I, and put yourself last

mistakes.wrong: I like this song. ~ I too.
mistakes.right: I like this song. ~ Me too.

points.title: Than me or than I am? Between you and me
points.summary: After ***than*** and ***as***, use an **object pronoun** in everyday English (*She's taller than me*) or **subject + verb** in careful English (*She's taller than I am*). After prepositions like ***between*** and ***except***, always use the **object** form: *between you and me*.

rows: *He's older **than me**. She's as tall **as him**.*
*He's older **than I am**. She's as tall **as he is**.*

blocks.md: *Than I* without a verb (*He's older than I*) is very formal and sounds old-fashioned. Use *than me* or *than I am*.
***Between you and me*** = this is a secret. *Between you and I* is a common mistake.

examples.text: My sister is younger **than I am**.
**Between you and me**, I don't like the new boss.

mistakes.wrong: Between you and I, he's leaving the company.
mistakes.right: Between you and me, he's leaving the company.

mistakes.wrong: Nobody except he knew the answer.
mistakes.right: Nobody except him knew the answer.

topics.summary: Finished actions and situations in the past: I worked, she went, Did you see it?
intro: We use the **past simple** for actions and situations that **finished** in the past: *I **watched** a film last night. We **went** to Spain in 2022.*
Regular verbs add *-ed* (*work → worked*). Many common verbs are irregular (*go → went*). For the past of *be*, see [Was and Were](/blog/grammar/was-were/).

points.title: Regular verbs: -ed
points.summary: Add **-ed** to regular verbs: *work → worked, live → lived, study → studied, stop → stopped*. Same form for every person.

rows: work → work**ed**, want → want**ed**, play → play**ed**
live → live**d**, like → like**d**, dance → dance**d**
study → stud**ied**, try → tr**ied**, carry → carr**ied**
stop → sto**pped**, plan → pla**nned**, drop → dro**pped**

blocks.md: The form is the same for *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*: *I **worked**, she **worked**, they **worked**.*

**Pronunciation.** After *t* or *d*, *-ed* is an extra syllable /ɪd/: *want**ed**, need**ed**, start**ed***. After other sounds it is just /t/ or /d/: *work**ed** (/t/), play**ed** (/d/)*. Don't say *work-ed*.

examples.text: We **lived** in Toronto for three years.

points.title: Irregular verbs
points.summary: Many common verbs have a special past form: *go → went, have → had, see → saw, buy → bought*. Learn them as words.

blocks.md: Irregular verbs don't add *-ed*. You need to learn their past forms. Here are some of the most common:
Like regular verbs, the past form is the same for every person: *I **went**, she **went**, they **went**.*
Some verbs don't change at all: *put → put, cut → cut, cost → cost, hit → hit, let → let*. *Read* is written the same but pronounced differently: *read* (/riːd/) → *read* (/red/).

examples.text: We **went** to the beach on Saturday.
She **bought** a new laptop last week.

points.title: Didn't and did… ? (negatives and questions)
points.summary: Negative: **didn't + base verb**. Question: **Did + subject + base verb?** *I didn't go. Did you go?*

blocks.md: After *didn't* and *did*, use the **base verb** (no *-ed*, no irregular past): *She **didn't go**.* Not *She didn't went*.
When *who* or *what* is the **subject**, don't use *did*: ***Who called** you?* (Someone called you.) Compare: *Who **did** you **call**?* (You called someone.)

mistakes.why: Wh-question: where + did + subject + base verb.

points.title: Time words: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2010
points.summary: Use the past simple with **finished** time: *yesterday, last Monday, two years ago, in 2010, when I was young*.

rows: *yesterday, yesterday morning, the day before yesterday*
*last night, last week, last Monday, last year* (no *the*)
*ten minutes ago, three days ago, a long time ago* (after the time)
*in 2010, in May, on Friday, at 8 o'clock*
*when I was a child, when we lived in Paris*

blocks.md: ***Ago*** comes **after** the period of time: *I met her **two years ago**.* Not *before two years* or *ago two years*.
Say ***last night***, not *yesterday night*. Say ***last week***, not *the last week* (*the last week* means the seven days up to now).

Questions about finished time use *When…?* + past simple: ***When did** you **arrive**?* Not *When have you arrived?* See [Present Perfect vs Past Simple](/blog/grammar/present-perfect-vs-past-simple/).

examples.text: **When I was a child**, I lived near the sea.

mistakes.wrong: I met him before two weeks.
mistakes.right: I met him two weeks ago.

points.title: Telling a story: events in order
points.summary: Use the past simple for a series of finished events, one after another: *I got up, had a shower and left.*

blocks.md: When we tell what happened, one action after another, we use the past simple for each action: *She **opened** the door, **looked** around and **walked** in.*
Useful sequence words: *first, then, after that, next, later, finally, in the end.*
The past simple is also used for **past habits** and for **finished periods**: *I **walked** to school every day. She **worked** there for ten years* (she doesn't now).
Don't change tense in the middle of a story without a reason: *I went in and **sat** down.* Not *I went in and sit down.*

examples.text: We **arrived** at the hotel, **left** our bags and **went** to the beach.
First I **made** a coffee, then I **checked** my emails.
He **lived** in Japan for five years.
When I was a student, I **cycled** to class every day.

mistakes.wrong: I went home and cook dinner.
mistakes.right: I went home and cooked dinner.

points.title: Irregular verbs that are easy to mix up
points.summary: Some past forms look or sound similar: *fell / felt, thought / taught, bought / brought, left / lived, won / earned*.

blocks.md: These pairs cause many mistakes in writing and speaking: *I **fell** off my bike* (fall) is different from *I **felt** ill* (feel).
*Bought* (buy) and *brought* (bring) sound almost the same. *Brought* has an **r**, like *bring*: *I **brought** a cake to the party* (I carried it there). *I **bought** a cake* (I paid for it).

examples.text: He **brought** his guitar to the party.

points.title: Past forms that don't mean past
points.summary: The past simple can make requests softer (*I wondered if…*) and describe unreal situations (*It's time we left*).

blocks.md: Sometimes the past simple refers to the **present or future**, not the past. There are two main uses:

items: **Distance and politeness.** The past makes a request or question less direct: *I **wondered** if you could help me. **Did** you **want** to see me? I **hoped** you might have a minute.*

**Unreal situations.** After *if, wish, if only, it's time, would rather, suppose / imagine*: *If I **had** more time, I'd learn the piano. It's time we **went** home. I'd rather you **didn't tell** anyone.*

blocks.md: In both uses the meaning is *now* or *in the future*. *It's time we **went*** means we should go **now**.

The past continuous is even softer for requests: *I **was wondering** if you could help.* See [Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-continuous/). For the full picture of unreal past forms, see [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/).

examples.text: I **wondered** if you were free on Friday.
It's high time we **booked** our tickets.
I'd rather you **came** a bit earlier.

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather you don't smoke here.
mistakes.right: I'd rather you didn't smoke here.

topics.summary: How to make nouns plural (book → books, city → cities, child → children) and which verb to use with them.
intro: Most English nouns make the plural with ***-s***: *one book, two books*. But there are spelling rules (*box → boxes, city → cities*) and some common **irregular** plurals (*man → men, child → children*).
Some nouns are always plural (*jeans, scissors*), and some never take a plural at all. For those, see [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/).

points.title: Regular plurals: -s, -es, -ies, -ves
points.summary: Add **-s** to most nouns (*cars*). Add **-es** after *-s, -sh, -ch, -x* (*boxes*). Consonant + *y* → **-ies** (*cities*). Many *-f / -fe* words → **-ves** (*knives*).

rows: *bus → buses, class → classes, dish → dishes, watch → watches, box → boxes*
*knife → knives, leaf → leaves, wife → wives, half → halves*

blocks.md: **Pronunciation**: *-s* sounds like /s/ after /p, t, k, f/ (*books*), /z/ after most other sounds (*cars, days*), and /ɪz/ after /s, z, ʃ, tʃ, dʒ/ (*buses, watches, pages*).
Some *-f* words just add *-s*: *roofs, chefs, beliefs*.

examples.text: There are many big **cities** in Canada.

points.title: Irregular plurals: men, children, feet, people
points.summary: Some common nouns have **irregular** plurals: *man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice*. Some don't change: *sheep, fish*.

blocks.md: These nouns don't add *-s*, but they still take a **plural verb**: *The children **are** playing.*
*People* is the normal plural of *person*. (*Persons* is very formal, for example in legal notices.)

examples.text: Three **men** and two **women** got on the bus.
We saw a lot of **sheep** on the farm.

mistakes.wrong: There are many childs in the park.
mistakes.right: There are many children in the park.

mistakes.wrong: Ten persons came to the party.
mistakes.right: Ten people came to the party.

points.title: Always plural: jeans, scissors, clothes, police
points.summary: Some nouns are **always plural**: *trousers, jeans, glasses, scissors, clothes*. Use **a pair of** to count them. ***Police*** and ***people*** also take a plural verb.

blocks.md: These nouns take a **plural verb**: *My jeans **are** too tight. Where **are** my glasses?*
To count them, use ***a pair of***: *I bought **a pair of** jeans and **two pairs of** shoes.* (not *a jeans*)
*Police* is plural: ***The police are** looking for him.*

mistakes.right: I bought a new pair of trousers.

points.title: Group nouns: the team is or the team are?
points.summary: **Group nouns** like *family, team, government, staff, class* can take a **singular or plural verb** in British English (*The team is / are winning*). American English usually uses the singular.

blocks.md: Use a **singular** verb when you think of the group as **one unit**. In British English, a **plural** verb is common when you think of the **individual people**.
American English normally uses a singular verb: *The team **is** celebrating.*
Some group words are always plural: ***people, police, cattle***.
The pronoun matches the verb: *The company **has** changed **its** logo. / The team **are** proud of **their** coach.*

examples.text: Our class **is** the biggest in the school.

mistakes.wrong: The team are proud of its coach.
mistakes.right: The team are proud of their coach.

points.title: Criteria, crises, passers-by and the news is
points.summary: Greek and Latin plurals (*criterion → criteria, crisis → crises*), compound plurals (*passers-by*), nouns that are the same in the singular and plural (*series, species*), and singular nouns ending in *-s* (*news, physics*).

rows: *analysis → analyses, crisis → crises, thesis → theses, hypothesis → hypotheses*

blocks.md: ***Data*** is plural in formal scientific writing (*the data **are***), but most people use it as uncountable (*the data **is***). Both are accepted today.
These nouns end in *-s* but take a **singular** verb: ***news, maths, physics, economics, athletics***: *The news **is** good.*
In compound nouns, the **main** noun takes the *-s*: *passer**s**-by, mother**s**-in-law*.

examples.text: Several **criteria** were used to choose the winner.
There have been two economic **crises** this decade.

topics.summary: How to show who something belongs to: Ali's phone, my parents' house, the end of the film, a friend of mine.
intro: Add ***'s*** to a person to show that something belongs to them: *This is **Sara's** bag.* For plural nouns ending in *-s*, add just an **apostrophe**: *my **parents'** house*.
For possessive words like *my, his, mine* and *hers*, see [Possessive Pronouns](/blog/grammar/possessive-pronouns/).

points.title: 's and s': my sister's car, my parents' house
points.summary: Add **'s** to a person or animal to show possession: *Ali's phone, my sister's car*. For regular plurals ending in *-s*, add only an **apostrophe**: *my parents' house*. Irregular plurals take **'s**: *the children's toys*.

blocks.md: The thing that is owned comes **after** the possessive: *Ali's **book*** (not *the book of Ali*).
Don't confuse possessive *'s* with *'s* = *is* or *has*: *Ali**'s** tired* (= Ali is tired). *Ali**'s** car* (possessive).

examples.text: **My parents'** house is near the sea.

mistakes.wrong: This is the car of my father.
My parent's house is big. (two parents)

points.title: At the doctor's, Ali and Sara's house
points.summary: Use **'s** for **shops and homes** without the noun: *at the doctor's, at my aunt's*. When two people **share** something, add *'s* to the **second** name: *Ali and Sara's flat*. For **separate** things, add it to both: *Ali's and Sara's phones*.

rows: *I'm going to **the hairdresser's / the dentist's / the chemist's**.*
*We had dinner **at my aunt's**.* (= at my aunt's house)

blocks.md: In American English, people often say *the dentist, the doctor* without *'s*. Both are correct.

examples.text: I've got an appointment **at the dentist's**.
We stayed **at my cousin's** for a week.
**Reza and Mina's** baby was born yesterday.

mistakes.wrong: Ali's and Sara's wedding was lovely. (one wedding)
mistakes.right: Ali and Sara's wedding was lovely.

mistakes.wrong: We met at my grandma. (at her house)

points.title: 's or of? My friend's name, the end of the film
points.summary: Use **'s** mostly for **people and animals** (*my friend's name*). Use **of** for **parts of things** (*the end of the street, the top of the page*). Both are possible with **places and organisations** (*Canada's capital / the capital of Canada*).

rows: parts of things: *the top of the page, the back of the room*
*the middle of the night, the end of the film*
places, organisations: *Toronto's mayor, the company's profits*
*the mayor of Toronto, the profits of the company*
long description: *the son of the woman who lives next door*

blocks.md: With **things**, *of* or a **compound noun** is usually more natural: *the end of the street, the car door, the kitchen window*. With *top, bottom, back, front, middle, end*, use *of*: *the back **of** the room* (not *the room's back*).
With a **long** description of the person, use *of*: *the phone number **of** the man I met at the party*.

examples.text: I didn't understand **the end of the film**.
Write your name at **the top of the page**.

mistakes.wrong: I woke up in the night's middle.
mistakes.right: I woke up in the middle of the night.

mistakes.wrong: Let's sit at the room's back.
mistakes.right: Let's sit at the back of the room.

points.title: Today's news, a week's holiday, a friend of mine
points.summary: Use **'s / s'** with **time** expressions: *today's news, last week's meeting, a week's holiday, two hours' drive, in ten minutes' time*. Use **a friend of mine** or **a friend of my sister's** to mean *one of my friends*.

rows: *today's newspaper, yesterday's meeting, next month's exam*
*a week's holiday, an hour's drive, two weeks' notice, in five minutes' time*

blocks.md: With plural time words ending in *-s*, add only an apostrophe: *two **weeks'** holiday, three **days'** walk*.
***A friend of mine*** = one of my friends (I have more than one). *My friend* often means a particular friend the listener knows about.
A compound adjective with a hyphen is another common pattern: *a two-hour drive, a ten-minute walk*. See [Noun Modifiers and Compound Nouns](/blog/grammar/noun-modifiers-compound-nouns/).

examples.text: We had **a week's** holiday in Spain.
The hotel is **ten minutes'** walk from the beach.
**A friend of mine** works at Google.

mistakes.wrong: I read it in the today newspaper.
mistakes.right: I read it in today's newspaper.

points.title: Group possessives, else's, its and one's
points.summary: **'s** can attach to a whole **noun phrase**: *the King of Spain's visit, someone else's bag*. In formal writing, prefer *of* with long phrases. Possessive pronouns have **no apostrophe**: *its, hers, ours, theirs*.

rows: *the Prime Minister of Canada's speech, my brother-in-law's car*
*The company changed **its** name.* / ***It's*** (= it is) late.
*the man next door's dog* (informal) → *the dog that belongs to the man next door* (writing)

blocks.md: The *'s* goes at the **end of the whole phrase**, not on the main noun: *the head of department**'s** office* (not *the head's of department office*).
In formal writing, long *'s* phrases can sound clumsy. Use *of* or rephrase: *the speech **of** the Prime Minister of Canada* or *the Canadian Prime Minister's speech*.
Possessive **pronouns** never have an apostrophe: ***its, hers, ours, yours, theirs***.

examples.text: **The Queen of Denmark's** visit was a success.
