topics.summary: Saying where things are: in the box, on the table, at the door, under the bed, next to the window.
intro: **Prepositions of place** say **where** something is: *The keys are **on** the table. The cat is **under** the bed. I'm **at** the station.*
The three most important are ***in, on*** and ***at***, and they're also the most confusing. This page goes step by step.

points.title: In, on, under, next to, between, behind
points.summary: Basic prepositions of place: ***in*** (inside), ***on*** (on a surface), ***under, next to, between, behind, in front of, opposite, near***.

rows: *The car is **behind** the house. There's a tree **in front of** the house.*
*The school is **opposite** the park.* (on the other side of the road)

blocks.md: ***Next to*** and ***in front of*** need all their words: *next **to** the door, in front **of** the school*. ***Near*** doesn't need *to*: *near the door*.

mistakes.wrong: The book is in the table.
mistakes.right: The book is on the table.

mistakes.wrong: The park is in front the school.
mistakes.right: The park is in front of the school.

points.title: In, on or at? At the door, in the room, on the wall
points.summary: ***At*** = a **point** or a place where something happens (*at the bus stop, at work, at a party*). ***In*** = **inside** an area or space (*in the kitchen, in Toronto*). ***On*** = a **surface** or a **line** (*on the wall, on the second floor*).

rows: a point: *at the door, at the traffic lights*
inside: *in the box, in the car*
a surface: *on the table, on the wall*
an event or activity: *at a party, at work, at school*
a city or country: *in Tehran, in Canada*
a room or building (inside): *in the kitchen*
*on the left / right, on the map*

blocks.md: Use ***at*** for a building when you mean the **activity** or a **meeting point**: *I'll meet you **at** the cinema.* Use ***in*** when you mean **inside**: *It's cold **in** the cinema.*
***On*** + street (*on Queen Street*) but ***at*** + full address (*at 15 Queen Street*).

examples.text: I'll wait for you **at** the bus stop.
Our flat is **on** the fifth floor.

mistakes.wrong: My office is in the second floor.
mistakes.right: My office is on the second floor.

mistakes.wrong: There were 100 people in the party.
mistakes.right: There were 100 people at the party.

points.title: On the bus, in the car, arrive in or at
points.summary: Use ***on*** for public transport and bikes (*on the bus, on a plane, on my bike*) and ***in*** for cars and taxis (*in the car*). ***Arrive in*** a city or country; ***arrive at*** a building or place (*arrive at the airport*). Never *arrive to*.

rows: *I read **on the bus**. She came **on her bike**.*
*get on / off* the bus or train
***Get off** the bus at the next stop.*
*get in(to) / out of* the car or taxi

blocks.md: ***By*** + transport, with no *the*: *by bus, by car, by plane* (but *on foot*).

examples.text: I met him **on the train** to Montreal.
What time did you **arrive at** the airport?

mistakes.wrong: I arrived to the hotel late.
mistakes.right: I arrived at the hotel late.

mistakes.wrong: She was sitting on the car.
mistakes.right: She was sitting in the car.

mistakes.wrong: I go to work with bus.
mistakes.right: I go to work by bus.

points.title: Over, above, across, through, along, past
points.summary: ***Above / below*** = higher / lower. ***Over*** = above, often covering or moving to the other side. ***Across*** = from one side to the other of a flat surface. ***Through*** = inside, from one end to the other. ***Along*** = following a line. ***Past*** = going by.

rows: *The plane flew **above** the clouds. The temperature is **below** zero.*
*She put a blanket **over** the baby. He jumped **over** the wall.*
*The train went **through** the tunnel. We walked **through** the forest.*
*She jumped **into** the pool. Get **out of** the car.*

blocks.md: For **numbers** and levels, use ***above / below***: *above average, 10 degrees below zero*. ***Over*** often means *more than*: *over 100 people*.

mistakes.wrong: The cat jumped in the table.
mistakes.right: The cat jumped onto the table.

points.title: Under pressure, on the brink of, beyond repair
points.summary: Prepositions of place are often used **figuratively**: ***under*** pressure / control / construction, ***on the verge / brink of***, ***beyond*** repair / belief, ***within*** reach / walking distance, ***among*** (in a group).

rows: affected by / in the process of
*The company is **on the brink of** collapse.*
*She was **among** the winners.* (a group) / *a secret **between** you and me*
*the problem **at the heart of** the debate*

blocks.md: ***Between*** is for clearly separate things, often two; ***among*** is for a group or crowd: *The house is hidden **among** the trees.*

examples.text: The new bridge is still **under construction**.
The species is **on the verge of** extinction.

mistakes.wrong: The situation is in control now.
mistakes.right: The situation is under control now.

topics.h1: Prepositions of Time: In, On and At
topics.summary: When to use at (at 7 pm), on (on Friday) and in (in May), plus for, during, by, until and within.
intro: Use ***at*** for exact **times**, ***on*** for **days and dates**, and ***in*** for **longer periods** like months, years and seasons: *at 7 pm, on Friday, in May*.
This page also covers *for, during, by, until* and *within*. For *for* and *since*, see [For, Since and Ago](/blog/grammar/for-since/).

points.title: At 6 o'clock, on Monday, in July
points.summary: ***At*** + times (*at 6 o'clock, at night*), ***on*** + days and dates (*on Monday, on 5 May*), ***in*** + months, years, seasons and parts of the day (*in July, in 2025, in the morning*).

rows: times: *at 6 o'clock, at 7.30, at noon, at midnight*
*on Monday morning, on New Year's Day*
special days: *on Christmas Day, on my wedding day*
parts of the day: *in the morning / afternoon / evening*

blocks.md: American English often says ***on the weekend***; British English says ***at the weekend***. Both are correct.
Use **no preposition** before *this, next, last, every, today, tomorrow, yesterday*: *I'll see you **next** Friday.* (not *on next Friday*)

mistakes.wrong: The meeting is at next Tuesday.
I go to bed in midnight.
mistakes.right: I go to bed at midnight.

points.title: On Monday morning, at night, in ten minutes, on time
points.summary: ***In the morning***, but ***on*** + a specific day: ***on Monday morning***. ***At night*** (in general), but ***in the night*** (during one night). ***In*** + period = after that time from now: *in ten minutes*. ***On time*** = not late; ***in time*** = early enough.

rows: *The train leaves **in 10 minutes**.* (= 10 minutes from now)
*The bus was **on time**.* (at the planned time) / *We arrived **in time** for dinner.* (early enough)

blocks.md: ***On time*** = at the correct time, not late. ***In time*** = early enough for something.

mistakes.wrong: I have an exam in Monday morning.
mistakes.right: I have an exam on Monday morning.

mistakes.wrong: I'll call you after ten minutes. (from now)
mistakes.right: I'll call you in ten minutes.

mistakes.wrong: We got there on time to see the start.
mistakes.right: We got there in time to see the start.

points.title: For, during or while?
points.summary: ***For*** + a period says **how long** (*for two hours*). ***During*** + a noun says **when**, inside a period (*during the film*). ***While*** + a clause (subject + verb): *while I was watching the film*.

rows: *I fell asleep **while** I was watching the film.*

blocks.md: Don't use *during* to say how long: *I lived there **for** three years* (not *during three years*).

examples.text: We stayed in Paris **for** a week.
My phone rang **while** I was driving.

mistakes.wrong: I studied English during five years.
mistakes.right: I studied English for five years.

mistakes.wrong: During I was cooking, the phone rang.
mistakes.right: While I was cooking, the phone rang.

points.title: By or until? From… to, within
points.summary: ***Until / till*** = up to a time (an action **continues**): *I'll wait **until** 6.* ***By*** = **not later than** (a deadline): *Please finish it **by** Friday.* ***Within*** = before the end of a period: *within 24 hours*.

rows: before the end of a period

blocks.md: A quick test: *by* answers “what's the deadline?”; *until* answers “how long does it continue?”.
***By the time*** + clause: ***By the time** we arrived, the film had started.*

examples.text: I'll be at the office **until** six.
The essay must be submitted **by** Friday.

mistakes.wrong: Please pay until the end of the month.
mistakes.right: Please pay by the end of the month.

mistakes.wrong: I'll wait for you by 8 o'clock.
mistakes.right: I'll wait for you until 8 o'clock.

points.title: As of, over the last decade, on arrival
points.summary: Formal and advanced expressions: ***as of / as from*** (starting from), ***over*** + period (during the whole period), ***in the run-up to*** (in the period before), ***in the course of*** (during), ***on*** + noun / *-ing* (as soon as), ***at the turn of the century***.

rows: ***In the course of** the meeting, three issues came up.*
***On arrival**, please go to reception. **On hearing** the news, she cried.*
*The house was built **at the turn of the century**.*

blocks.md: ***On*** + *-ing* is formal and means *as soon as*: ***On receiving** your payment, we will send the goods.* (*Upon* is even more formal.)

examples.text: **As of** today, the office is closed on Fridays.
Unemployment has fallen **over** the past two years.
**On arrival**, guests will receive a welcome drink.
Prices rose **in the run-up to** Christmas.

mistakes.wrong: In arrival, please show your ticket.
mistakes.right: On arrival, please show your ticket.

mistakes.wrong: As of from Monday, the new rules apply.
mistakes.right: As of Monday, the new rules apply.

topics.summary: Now, around now, plans and changes: I'm working, are you coming?
intro: We use the **present continuous** for actions happening **now** or **around now**: *I**'m reading** a book. She**'s studying** for her exams this week.*
Form it with **am / is / are + verb-ing**. At higher levels it is also used for future plans, changing situations and annoying habits.

points.title: Form and use: I'm working (now)
points.summary: am / is / are + verb-ing for something happening at the moment of speaking.

rows: I**'m working**. He**'s sleeping**. They**'re playing**.
I**'m not working**. She **isn't sleeping**. We **aren't playing**.
Yes, + subject + am / is / are. / No, + subject + 'm not / isn't / aren't.
Yes, I am. / No, she isn't.
question word + **am / is / are** + subject + verb-ing?
work → working, read → reading, play → playing
Verb ends in **-e**: drop the e
make → making, write → writing, come → coming
One vowel + one consonant at the end of a stressed syllable: double the consonant
run → running, sit → sitting, swim → swimming, stop → stopping
Verb ends in **-ie**: change ie to **-ying**
lie → lying, die → dying, tie → tying

blocks.md: Use it for something happening **at the moment of speaking**. Common words: *now, right now, at the moment, Look!, Listen!*

In speaking we usually use contractions: *I'm, you're, he's, she's, it's, we're, they're.* British and American spelling differ for some verbs ending in -l: *travelling* (UK) / *traveling* (US). Both are correct.

examples.text: He**'s sitting** next to the window.

mistakes.wrong: She is work at the moment.
mistakes.right: She is working at the moment.

points.title: Around now and temporary situations
points.summary: Use the present continuous for things happening around now (this week, at the moment) and temporary situations.

blocks.md: The action can be happening **around now**, not exactly at this second: *I**'m reading** a great book at the moment.* (Maybe I'm not reading it right now, but I've started and haven't finished.)
It's also used for **temporary** situations: *My cousin **is staying** with us this month. Sam **is working** from home this week.*
Common words: *at the moment, today, this week, this month, this year, currently.*

examples.text: I**'m reading** a great book at the moment.
My cousin **is staying** with us this month.
We**'re learning** about volcanoes in class this week.

mistakes.wrong: I read a really good book at the moment.
mistakes.right: I'm reading a really good book at the moment.

mistakes.wrong: My sister stays with us this month.
mistakes.right: My sister is staying with us this month.

points.title: Future arrangements: I'm meeting Sam tonight
points.summary: Use the present continuous for future plans that are already arranged, usually with a time.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for **future arrangements**: plans you've already made, often with a time, a place or other people: *I**'m meeting** Sam at 6 tonight. We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.*
Common words: *tonight, tomorrow, on Friday, next week, at the weekend.*
*Be going to* is also correct for plans: *I'm going to meet Sam at 6.* For timetables, use the present simple: *The film **starts** at 8.* See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

examples.text: We**'re flying** to Rome on Monday.
She**'s starting** her new job next week.

mistakes.wrong: I see the dentist tomorrow. (my appointment)
What do you do this weekend?
mistakes.right: What are you doing this weekend?

points.title: Changing situations: It's getting colder
points.summary: Use the present continuous for situations that are changing now: get, become, increase, improve.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for a **change that is happening** at the moment: *The weather **is getting** colder. Prices **are rising**.*
Verbs often used this way: *get, become, change, improve, increase, rise, fall, grow, start, begin.* *Get* + comparative is very common: *It's **getting darker**. Your English is **getting better**.*

examples.text: I**'m starting** to enjoy my new job.

mistakes.wrong: The population increases very fast at the moment.
mistakes.right: The population is increasing very fast at the moment.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

mistakes.wrong: It gets dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.right: It's getting dark. Let's go home.
mistakes.why: A change happening now: present continuous.

points.title: always + continuous: He's always complaining
points.summary: always / constantly / forever + continuous for something that happens too often, often annoying.

blocks.md: *Always, constantly* or *forever* + present continuous means something happens **very often, often too often**. We usually use it to complain: *He**'s always complaining**. You**'re forever losing** your keys!*
Compare: *I **always walk** to work* = every time, a normal habit (neutral).
Word order: **be + always + verb-ing**: *She**'s always interrupting** me.* (not *always is interrupting*)

examples.text: My neighbour **is constantly playing** loud music.

mistakes.wrong: I'm always going to work by bike. (my normal habit)
mistakes.right: I always go to work by bike.
mistakes.why: For a neutral habit, use the present simple.

points.title: In progress at a regular time; always for typical behaviour
points.summary: At 8 I'm usually driving = in the middle of it at that time; always + continuous can also describe typical (even positive) behaviour.

blocks.md: Use the present continuous for an action that is **in progress at a regular time**: *At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast, so call me later.* Compare: *I usually **have** breakfast at 7* = that's when I start it.
*Always / constantly* + continuous describes **typical behaviour**. It's often a complaint, but it can also be positive: *My neighbour **is always bringing** us cakes. She's so kind.*

examples.text: At 7 a.m. I**'m usually having** breakfast.
Don't call between 6 and 7: we**'re usually eating** then.
On Saturday mornings I**'m normally working** in the garden.
Whenever I visit, he**'s watching** TV.

mistakes.wrong: At 8 I'm usually drive to work.
mistakes.right: At 8 I'm usually driving to work.

points.title: When not to use it for the future
points.summary: Use the present continuous for arranged or decided plans, not for predictions or permanent future situations.

blocks.md: The present continuous for the future suggests something **arranged or firmly decided**: *I**'m not lending** him my car again.* So we don't use it for:

items: **Predictions** about things nobody can arrange, like the weather: *It**'s going to rain** tonight. / It**'ll rain** tonight.* (not *It's raining tonight*)
**Permanent** future situations: *People **will live** longer in the future.* (not *are living longer in the future*)

blocks.md: With **go** and **come**, many people prefer the present continuous to *going to go / going to come*: *I**'m going** to town on Saturday. **Are** you **coming** home for lunch?*

examples.text: I**'m going** to Toronto next week.
I**'m not lending** him my car again.

mistakes.right: It's going to rain tomorrow. / It'll rain tomorrow.
mistakes.why: The weather can't be arranged: use going to or will.

mistakes.wrong: In the future, people are living on other planets.
mistakes.right: In the future, people will live on other planets.
mistakes.why: Predictions about the future: will or going to.

topics.summary: Habits, facts, timetables and more: I work, she works, do you work?
intro: We use the **present simple** for habits, routines and things that are generally true: *I **drink** coffee every morning. The sun **rises** in the east.*
With **he, she, it**, add **-s** to the verb: *She **works** in a bank.* For negatives and questions, use **do / does**: *I **don't** like fish. **Does** he **speak** French?*

points.title: Form: I work, she works
points.summary: Use the base verb with I, you, we, they; add -s or -es with he, she, it.

rows: work → works, read → reads, live → lives
kiss → kisses, wash → washes, watch → watches, fix → fixes, go → goes, do → does
study → studies, try → tries, fly → flies
play → plays, buy → buys, enjoy → enjoys

blocks.md: **Be** is different: *I **am**, you **are**, she **is**.* Don't use *am / is / are* with another verb in the present simple: *I **work*** (not *I am work*).

points.title: Negatives and questions: don't, doesn't, do, does
points.summary: Negatives: don't / doesn't + base verb. Questions: do / does + subject + base verb.

blocks.md: Use **-s** only once. After *doesn't* and *does*, use the base verb: *She doesn't **work**. Does she **work**?* (not *doesn't works*)
Keep the question order: question word + *do / does* + subject + verb: *What **does** this word **mean**?* (not *What means this word?*)

examples.text: We **don't watch** TV in the morning.

mistakes.why: After doesn't, use the base verb.
After does, use the base verb.

points.title: Uses: habits, facts and permanent situations
points.summary: Use the present simple for habits, routines, facts, permanent situations and likes.

items: Habits and routines: *I **get up** at 7 o'clock. We **play** football on Saturdays.*
Facts and things that are always true: *Water **boils** at 100°C. The sun **rises** in the east.*
Permanent situations: *My parents **live** in Toronto. She **works** for a big company.*
Likes, dislikes and opinions: *I **love** pizza. He **doesn't like** cold weather.*

blocks.md: Common time words: *every day, every week, on Mondays, in the morning, twice a week.* Ask about frequency with ***How often**…?*: *How often **do** you **go** to the gym?*

*Always, usually, often, sometimes, never* go **before** the main verb but **after** *be*: *I **usually** walk to work. He**'s always** late.* See [Adverbs of Frequency](/blog/grammar/adverbs-of-frequency/).

examples.text: I **love** pizza, but I **don't like** pasta.
How often **do** you **go** to the gym? – Twice a week.

mistakes.why: Adverbs of frequency go after be.

mistakes.wrong: I go every day to work.
mistakes.right: I go to work every day.
mistakes.why: Time words like every day usually go at the end.
For facts that are always true, use the present simple.

points.title: Timetables and schedules: The train leaves at 8
points.summary: Use the present simple for future events on a timetable or schedule.

blocks.md: Use the present simple for **future** events that are on a timetable or a fixed schedule: transport, films, classes, opening times. *The train **leaves** at 8:30 tomorrow. What time **does** the film **start** tonight?*

For **your own plans** with other people, use the present continuous or *be going to*, not the present simple: *I**'m meeting** Sam tonight.* (not *I meet Sam tonight*). See [Future Forms](/blog/grammar/future-forms/).

After *when, as soon as, before, after, until*, use the present simple for the future: *I'll call you when I **get** home.* (not *when I will get*). See [Future Time Clauses](/blog/grammar/future-time-clauses/).

examples.text: I'll text you when the plane **lands**.

mistakes.wrong: I meet my friends tonight. (my plan)
I'll call you when I will get home.
mistakes.right: I'll call you when I get home.
mistakes.why: After when, use the present simple for the future.

points.title: I promise, I agree, I apologise: saying is doing
points.summary: Verbs like promise, agree and apologise do the action when you say them: use the present simple.

blocks.md: Some verbs **perform an action** when you say them. When you say *I promise*, you make a promise. With these verbs, use the present simple, not the continuous: *I **promise** I won't be late.* (not *I'm promising*)
Common verbs: *promise, agree, apologise, suggest, advise, insist, admit, refuse, warn, thank, congratulate, request.*
To sound more polite or formal, add a modal: *I **would suggest** leaving early. I **must insist** that you stay. We **would advise** you to book in advance.*

examples.text: I **would advise** you to book early.

mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.
Agree is a verb: don't add am.

mistakes.wrong: I am apologising for the mistake.
mistakes.why: Saying it is the action: present simple.

points.title: Headlines, summaries, instructions and I hear
points.summary: The present simple is also used in headlines, plot summaries, instructions and to pass on news (I hear, I gather).

items: **Headlines** use the present simple for recent events: *Floods **hit** northern Italy. Minister **resigns**.*
**Summaries** of books, films and plays: *In the film, a young doctor **moves** to a small town and **discovers** a secret.*
**Instructions and demonstrations**: *First you **heat** the oil, then you **add** the onions.*
**Passing on news** with *I hear, I gather, I understand, they say, (someone) tells me*: *I **hear** you're moving to Vancouver. Anna **tells** me you've got a new job.*

blocks.md: In these uses, the present simple doesn't mean *now* or *regularly*. It's a convention that makes the text short and lively. In a summary, stay in the present simple: don't switch to the past in the middle.

examples.text: In chapter 3, the author **compares** the two cities.
First you **mix** the flour and the eggs.
I **gather** the meeting has been cancelled.
My doctor **tells** me I need more exercise.

mistakes.wrong: In the film, the hero moves to London and was finding a job.
mistakes.right: In the film, the hero moves to London and finds a job.
mistakes.why: In a summary, keep the present simple.

mistakes.wrong: Anna is telling me you're engaged.
mistakes.why: To pass on news, use tells me.

topics.summary: How to make questions: Are you…? Do you…? Where do you live? Who called you? What is it like? Don't you like it?
intro: In English questions, the **auxiliary verb** (*be, do, have, can, will…*) usually comes **before** the subject: ***Are** you hungry? **Do** you like tea? **Can** she swim?*

With question words (*what, where, when…*), the word goes first: ***Where do** you live?* This page goes from basic questions to negative and echo questions. For *Do you know where…?*, see [Indirect Questions](/blog/grammar/indirect-questions/).

points.title: Yes/no questions: Are you…? Do you…? Can you…?
points.summary: Put **be** or an **auxiliary** (*do, does, did, can, will, have*) before the subject: *Are you ready? Does she work here? Can you swim?*

blocks.md: With *be* and modals, just change the order. With other verbs, add ***do / does / did*** and use the **base verb**: ***Does** she **like** it?* Not *Does she likes it?*
Short answers repeat the auxiliary: *Yes, she **does**. / No, I **can't**. / Yes, they **are**.*

examples.text: **Did** they win the match? ~ No, they **didn't**.

points.title: Wh- question words: what, where, when, who, why, how
points.summary: Put the question word **first**, then the auxiliary and the subject: *Where do you live? What is your name? Why did she leave?*

blocks.md: Order: **question word + auxiliary / be + subject + main verb**: ***Where do** you **work**?* ***What are** you **doing**?*

mistakes.right: What time does the film start?

points.title: How much, how many, how long, how often, how far
points.summary: **How + adjective / adverb** asks about amount, time and frequency: *How much is it? How long does it take? How often do you exercise?*

blocks.md: ***How long does it take** (to…)?* asks about the time a journey or job needs: *How long does it take to get to the airport? ~ It takes about 40 minutes.*
***How much*** goes with uncountable nouns (*money, time, water*); ***how many*** with plural nouns (*people, books*).

examples.text: **How many** brothers and sisters do you have?
**How long** does it take to walk there?
**How often** do you visit your parents?

mistakes.wrong: How many money do you have?
mistakes.right: How much money do you have?

mistakes.wrong: How long it takes to get there?
mistakes.right: How long does it take to get there?

points.title: Who saw you? or Who did you see? Subject and object questions
points.summary: When **who / what** is the **subject**, don't use *do / did*: *Who called you?* When it's the **object**, use *do / did*: *Who did you call?*

blocks.md: Ask yourself: is the question word the person or thing that **does** the action? If yes, it's the **subject**: use normal word order, no *do*: ***Who broke** the window? ~ Tom did.*
If the question word is the person or thing that **receives** the action, use *do / does / did*: ***Who did** Tom **see**? ~ He saw Maria.*

mistakes.wrong: Who did break the window? (asking who did it)
Who you saw at the party?
mistakes.right: Who did you see at the party?

points.title: Who is she talking to? What is it like? Prepositions at the end
points.summary: In questions, prepositions usually go at the **end**: *Who are you talking **to**? Where are you **from**?* **What is it like?** = describe it.

blocks.md: When a verb has a preposition (*talk to, look at, come from, wait for, think about*), the preposition goes at the **end** of the question: *What are you looking **at**? Who is this present **for**?*
***What is … like?*** asks for a **description**: *What's your new school **like**? ~ It's big and modern.* It's different from *Do you like…?* (Do you enjoy it?)
In very formal English, the preposition can go first: ***To whom** did you speak?* In normal English, *Who did you speak to?* is much more common.

mistakes.wrong: How is your new boss like?
mistakes.right: What is your new boss like?

points.title: What or which? What kind of…?
points.summary: **which** = a choice from a small, known group: *Which colour do you want, red or blue?* **what** = an open choice: *What colour is your car?*

blocks.md: Use ***which*** when there is a **limited** number of options, often mentioned or obvious: ***Which** of these bags is yours? **Which** way is the station, left or right?*
Use ***what*** for an **open** question with many possible answers: ***What** music do you like? **What** time is it?*
***Which one(s)?*** and ***which of*** + plural: ***Which one** do you want? **Which of** your friends is coming?* (Not *what of*.)
***What kind of / what sort of*** asks about a type: ***What kind of** films do you like?*

examples.text: **Which** do you prefer, tea or coffee?
**What** do you want for your birthday?
**Which of** these photos do you like best?
**What kind of** job are you looking for?

points.title: Negative questions: Don't you…? Isn't it…?
points.summary: Negative questions (*Don't you…? Isn't it…? Haven't you…?*) show **surprise**, ask for **agreement**, or check something we **expect** to be true.

blocks.md: Negative questions are used:

items: for **surprise**: ***Don't** you **like** chocolate?* (I'm surprised.)
to ask for **agreement**: ***Isn't** it a beautiful day?* (I think it is.)
to check what we **expect**: ***Haven't** we **met** before?* (I think we have.)
in **complaints**: ***Can't** you be quiet?*

blocks.md: Answering: answer about the **fact**, not the question form: *Don't you like coffee? ~ **No**, I don't. (= I don't like it) / **Yes**, I do. (= I like it)*
In formal English, *not* can go after the subject: ***Do you not** agree?*

mistakes.wrong: Don't you like it? ~ No, I like it.
mistakes.right: Don't you like it? ~ Yes, I do. / Yes, I like it.

points.title: Echo questions and statement questions: You did what?
points.summary: **Echo questions** repeat part of what someone said to show surprise or check: *She's moving to Peru. ~ She's moving where?* **Statement questions** keep normal word order with rising intonation: *You're leaving?*

blocks.md: An **echo question** repeats the sentence and replaces the surprising part with a question word, with strong stress: *I paid $500 for it. ~ You paid **how much**?* *He married his boss. ~ He married **who**?*

A **statement question** uses normal word order with **rising** intonation. It checks or expresses surprise about something we think we heard or understood: *You've finished **already**?* *So you're not coming?*
Short **reply questions** show interest: *I've just got engaged. ~ **Have you**? Congratulations!* See [So Do I, Neither Do I](/blog/grammar/so-do-i-neither-do-i/).
These are spoken forms. In writing, use normal questions, except in dialogue.

examples.text: I've sold the car. ~ You've sold **what**?
You're not hungry? I made a huge dinner!
He's 90. ~ **Is he**? He looks much younger.

mistakes.wrong: You paid how much? (in a formal essay)

topics.h1: Requests, Offers and Permission (Can you…? May I…? Shall I…?)
topics.summary: Asking for things politely: Can you help me? Could I borrow your pen? Shall I open the window? Would you mind waiting?
intro: Modal verbs help us ask for things, offer help and ask for permission **politely**: ***Could** you help me? **May** I come in? **Shall** I carry that for you?*
In English, how polite you sound depends a lot on the words you choose. This page goes from simple requests to very polite and formal ones.

points.title: Can you…? Could you…? Asking someone to do something
points.summary: **Can you…?** and **Could you…?** + base verb ask someone to do something. *Could* is more polite: *Could you close the door, please?*

blocks.md: To ask **someone to do** something, use *Can / Could / Would you* + base verb: ***Could** you **speak** more slowly, please?*
To ask **for something**, use ***Can I have…?*** or ***Could I have…?***: ***Can I have** a glass of water, please?*
Add ***please*** to sound more polite. Common answers: *Sure. / Of course. / No problem. / Sorry, I can't.*

points.title: Can I…? Could I…? May I…? Asking for permission
points.summary: **Can I…?** (informal), **Could I…?** (polite) and **May I…?** (formal) ask for permission: *May I come in?*

blocks.md: ***May I…?*** is the most formal. It's common in shops, offices and with people you don't know well.
To **give** permission, use *can* or *may* (not *could*): *Yes, you **can**.* / *You **may** go now.* (formal)
Don't answer *Could I…?* with *Yes, you could*. Say *Yes, you **can**.* or *Of course.*

examples.text: You **can** use my computer if you like.

mistakes.wrong: Could I open the window? ~ Yes, you could.
mistakes.right: Could I open the window? ~ Yes, of course. / Yes, you can.
mistakes.why: Give permission with can, not could.

points.title: Offers and suggestions: Shall I…? Shall we…? Would you like…?
points.summary: Offers: **Shall I…? / Can I…? / I'll…** Suggestions: **Shall we…? / Let's… / Why don't we…?** Invitations: **Would you like…?**

rows: ***Shall I** open the window? **Can I** help you? **I'll** carry that.*
***Shall we** go out tonight? **Let's** take a taxi. **Why don't we** eat here?*
***Would you like to** come to dinner?*

blocks.md: ***Shall I / shall we*** + base verb is used for offers and suggestions, mostly in British English: ***Shall I** call a taxi?* In American English, people often say ***Should I…?*** or ***Do you want me to…?***
***I'll*** + base verb makes an offer at the moment of speaking: *You look busy. **I'll** make dinner.*
*Let's* + base verb (no *to*): ***Let's go*** (not *Let's to go*). Negative: ***Let's not*** argue.

mistakes.wrong: Let's to go to the beach.

points.title: Would you mind…? Do you mind if…?
points.summary: **Would you mind + -ing?** = a polite request. **Do you mind if I + present / Would you mind if I + past** = asking for permission. Answer *No, not at all* to say yes!

rows: ***Do you mind if I sit** here?*
***Would you mind if I opened** the window?*

blocks.md: *Mind* means *object to* (not like). So the polite answer **yes** is ***No, not at all*** / ***No, go ahead*** / ***Of course not***: *Do you mind if I sit here? ~ **No, not at all.*** (= Yes, you can.)
If you do mind, say something like: *Actually, I'd rather you didn't. / Sorry, that seat is taken.*

examples.text: **Do you mind if I open** the window? ~ No, go ahead.
**Would you mind if I left** a bit early?

mistakes.wrong: Would you mind to close the door?
mistakes.right: Would you mind closing the door?

mistakes.wrong: Do you mind if I sit here? ~ Yes, sure! (meaning you can)
mistakes.right: Do you mind if I sit here? ~ No, not at all.
mistakes.why: No = I don't mind = you can.

points.title: Be allowed to: permission and rules
points.summary: **be allowed to + verb** = have permission: *We **are allowed to** use phones at break.* Past: **was allowed to** / **could** (general). Rules: **not allowed to**.

blocks.md: ***Be allowed to*** describes permission given by someone else or by a rule: *Students **are allowed to** use dictionaries in the exam. You**'re not allowed to** smoke here.*
It works in all tenses: *Will we **be allowed to** take photos? I **wasn't allowed to** go out late when I was a teenager.*

For **general** permission in the past, *could* is also possible: *When I was a child, I **could** stay up late at weekends.* For **one particular** occasion, use ***was allowed to***: *I **was allowed to** leave early yesterday.* (not *I could leave early yesterday* for a single permitted action)

examples.text: Children **aren't allowed to** swim without an adult.
My parents **allowed** me **to** travel alone when I was 16.
Will I **be allowed to** bring my dog?

mistakes.wrong: We are not allow to eat here.
mistakes.right: We are not allowed to eat here.
I'm allowed to bring a guest.

points.title: Very polite requests: I was wondering if…, Would it be possible…?
points.summary: Indirect forms make requests softer and more formal: *I was wondering if you could…, Would it be possible to…?, Do you think you could…?, I'd appreciate it if you could…*

rows: ***Do you think you could** help me move on Saturday?*
***I was wondering if you could** check my CV.*
***Would it be possible to** change my appointment?*
*I'd be grateful / I'd appreciate it if you could…*
***I'd appreciate it if you could** reply by Friday.*
*Would you be so kind as to…?* (very formal)
***Would you be so kind as to** close the door?*

blocks.md: The longer and more indirect the request, the more polite it sounds. These forms are useful in emails, at work and when asking for a big favour.
Notice the **word order**: these are not direct questions inside: *I was wondering if you **could** help* (not *if could you help*).
Very formal phrases (*Would you be so kind as to…*) can sound sarcastic in casual situations. Choose the level of politeness that fits the situation.

examples.text: **I was wondering if** you **could** give me a lift.
**Would it be possible to** pay by card?
**I'd be grateful if** you **could** send me the details.
**Do you think you could** lower the music a little?

mistakes.wrong: I was wondering if could you help me.
mistakes.right: I was wondering if you could help me.

mistakes.wrong: I'd appreciate if you could reply.
mistakes.right: I'd appreciate it if you could reply.

topics.h1: Short Answers, So Do I, Neither Do I, I Think So
topics.summary: Short replies with auxiliary verbs: Yes, I do. So am I. Neither can I. Have you? I think so.
intro: In conversation, we often answer with just the **auxiliary verb** instead of repeating the whole sentence: *Do you like jazz? ~ Yes, I **do**. I'm tired. ~ So **am** I.*
This makes English sound natural and less repetitive. The auxiliary must match the verb in the first sentence: *be → am / is / are*, present simple → *do / does*, past simple → *did*, and so on.

points.title: Short answers: Yes, I do. No, she isn't.
points.summary: Answer yes/no questions with **Yes / No + pronoun + auxiliary**: *Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I **am**. Do they live here? ~ No, they **don't**.*

blocks.md: Use the **same auxiliary** as in the question. Don't contract positive short answers: *Yes, I **am**.* Not *Yes, I'm*.
A short answer alone (*Yes.*) can sound abrupt. *Yes, I do* is more polite and natural.

examples.text: Are you from Iran? ~ Yes, I **am**.
Does your brother work? ~ No, he **doesn't**.
Did you enjoy the film? ~ Yes, we **did**.
Will you be home tonight? ~ No, I **won't**.

mistakes.right: Are you hungry? ~ Yes, I am.
mistakes.why: no contraction in positive short answers

mistakes.wrong: Do you like it? ~ Yes, I like.
mistakes.right: Do you like it? ~ Yes, I do.
Is it cold? ~ Yes, it is.

points.title: So do I, Neither can I, Me too, Me neither
points.summary: To agree: **So + auxiliary + I** (positive): *I'm hungry. ~ So am I.* **Neither + auxiliary + I** (negative): *I can't swim. ~ Neither can I.*

blocks.md: Word order: ***So / Neither + auxiliary + subject***: *So **do I**. Neither **have we**.* Not *So I do*.
***Nor*** is also used like *neither*, especially in British English: *I don't like it. ~ **Nor do I**.*
To **disagree**, use the opposite auxiliary: *I love horror films. ~ Really? I **don't**. / I don't like coffee. ~ Oh, I **do**.*

examples.text: We went to the concert. ~ **So did we**.
I haven't seen it. ~ **Neither have I**.
I can't wait for the holidays. ~ **Me neither**!

mistakes.wrong: I like tea. ~ So I do.
mistakes.right: I like tea. ~ So do I.

mistakes.wrong: I don't eat meat. ~ So don't I.
mistakes.right: I don't eat meat. ~ Neither do I.

points.title: Reply questions: Have you? Really? Is she?
points.summary: Short **reply questions** (*Have you? Did she? Is it?*) show interest or surprise: *I've just got married! ~ Have you? Congratulations!*

blocks.md: To show you're **listening** and **interested**, reply with *auxiliary + pronoun* as a question: *I live in Calgary. ~ **Do you**? I've been there!*
The auxiliary matches the statement: positive → positive, negative → negative: *I don't eat meat. ~ **Don't you**? I didn't know that.*
Your intonation shows your feeling: rising for interest or surprise, falling for something you already guessed.

examples.text: I'm learning Japanese. ~ **Are you**? That's great!
She passed her driving test. ~ **Did she**? Wow!
I can't swim. ~ **Can't you**? I'll teach you!
We've bought a house. ~ **Have you**? Where?

mistakes.wrong: I've been to Peru. ~ Did you?
mistakes.right: I've been to Peru. ~ Have you?

mistakes.wrong: She lives in Rome. ~ Is she?
mistakes.right: She lives in Rome. ~ Does she?

points.title: I think so, I hope so, I'm afraid not, I don't think so
points.summary: Use **so** / **not** instead of repeating a clause: *Is it going to rain? ~ I hope not. Will she come? ~ I think so.*

blocks.md: ***So*** replaces a positive clause: *Is the shop open? ~ I **think so**.* (= I think it's open.)

With *think, expect, believe, suppose*, the negative is usually ***I don't think so***. With ***hope*** and ***be afraid***, use ***not***: *I **hope not**. I'm **afraid not**.* (not *I don't hope so*)

examples.text: Will it be sunny tomorrow? ~ I **hope so**.
Are we late? ~ I **don't think so**.
Did you lose the match? ~ I'm **afraid so**.
Can you come on Friday? ~ I'm **afraid not**.

mistakes.wrong: Will it rain? ~ I don't hope so.
mistakes.right: Will it rain? ~ I hope not.

mistakes.wrong: Is it true? ~ I think it.
mistakes.right: Is it true? ~ I think so.

points.title: Using auxiliaries to avoid repetition: She can, but I can't
points.summary: Use an **auxiliary** alone to avoid repeating a verb phrase: *I haven't seen it, but my brother **has**. She speaks French and **so does** her son.*

blocks.md: After the first clause, the auxiliary can stand for the whole verb phrase: *I wasn't tired, but everyone else **was**.* (= was tired)
Use *do / does / did* for simple tenses: *I don't like coffee, but my wife **does**. He said he'd call, and he **did**.*
This is common in contrasts with ***but***, additions with ***and so / and neither***, and replies: *Who can help? ~ I **can**.*

examples.text: I can't swim, but my sister **can**.
We don't eat meat, and **neither do** our kids.

mistakes.wrong: I don't smoke, but my dad smokes does.
mistakes.right: I don't smoke, but my dad does.

mistakes.wrong: She's tired and so I am.
mistakes.right: She's tired and so am I.

points.title: Nor, so it is, and other auxiliary patterns
points.summary: **Nor** + inversion adds a negative point formally (*He didn't apologise, nor did he explain*). **So it is / So I did** confirms with surprise. Stressed **do** adds emphasis (*I do like it!*).

blocks.md: ***Nor / neither + auxiliary + subject*** can join two negative ideas in formal speech and writing: *The government didn't reduce taxes, **nor did it** increase spending.*
***So + subject + auxiliary*** (no inversion) **confirms** something with surprise: *Look, it's snowing! ~ **So it is**!* (= You're right, it is!) Compare *So is it* (= it is too).
A stressed ***do / does / did*** in a positive sentence adds **emphasis** or contrast: *I **do** like your new haircut! She **did** call you, I promise.*

examples.text: I didn't see the accident, **nor did** anyone else.
You've got paint on your shirt. ~ Oh, **so I have**!
He doesn't like sport, **nor does** he watch it.

mistakes.wrong: He didn't call, nor he wrote.
mistakes.right: He didn't call, nor did he write.

mistakes.wrong: Look, the sun is out! ~ So is it!
mistakes.right: Look, the sun is out! ~ So it is!

Is your sister married? ~ No, she ___.

topics.summary: When to use some and any: I've got some money. Have you got any money? I haven't got any money.
intro: ***Some*** and ***any*** talk about an amount that isn't exact. Use them with **plural** nouns (*some eggs*) and **uncountable** nouns (*some milk*).

The basic rule is ***some*** in positive sentences and ***any*** in negatives and questions, but there are important exceptions. For countable and uncountable nouns, see [Countable and Uncountable Nouns](/blog/grammar/countable-uncountable-nouns/).

points.title: Some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **positive** sentences (*I've got some apples*). Use ***any*** in **negatives** (*I haven't got any apples*) and most **questions** (*Have you got any apples?*).

blocks.md: Use *some / any* with **plural** and **uncountable** nouns. With a singular countable noun, use *a / an*: *Is there **a** bank near here?* (not *any bank*)

examples.text: Are there **any** good restaurants near here?

mistakes.wrong: There are any chairs in the room.
mistakes.right: There are some chairs in the room.

points.title: Some in offers and requests: Can I have some water?
points.summary: Use ***some*** in **questions** when you **offer** something or **ask for** something, or when you expect the answer *yes*: *Would you like **some** coffee? Can I have **some** water?*

rows: *Can I have **some** water, please? Could you lend me **some** money?*
*Did you buy **some** bread?* (I think you did.)

blocks.md: Compare: *Have you got **any** questions?* (an open question) / *Would you like **some** more tea?* (an offer).

examples.text: Can I have **some** more rice, please?

mistakes.wrong: Can I have any water, please?
mistakes.right: Can I have some water, please?

points.title: Someone, anything, nowhere, everybody
points.summary: ***Some-, any-, no-, every-*** combine with ***-one / -body*** (people), ***-thing*** (things) and ***-where*** (places): *someone, anything, nowhere, everybody*. Use them like *some* and *any*.

blocks.md: ***No-*** words already have a negative meaning, so use a **positive** verb: *I saw **nobody**.* = *I didn't see **anybody**.* (not *I didn't see nobody*)
These words take a **singular** verb: ***Everyone is** here. **Nothing has** changed.*
Don't use *to* before *somewhere / anywhere* after *go*: *Let's go **somewhere** quiet.*

mistakes.wrong: I want to go to somewhere warm.
mistakes.right: I want to go somewhere warm.

points.title: Any = it doesn't matter which; any after if
points.summary: In **positive** sentences, ***any*** means **it doesn't matter which**: *Call me **any** time.* Use ***any*** after ***if*** and with words that have a **negative meaning** (*never, hardly, without*).

rows: *Choose **any** colour you like. **Anyone** can learn to cook.*

blocks.md: With this meaning, *any* can go with a **singular** noun: ***Any** child can do it. Take **any** bus from here.*
***Not… any*** = ***no***: *There **aren't any** chairs.* = *There **are no** chairs.* Use only **one** negative.

examples.text: **Any** bus from this stop goes to the centre.
There were **hardly any** people at the party.

mistakes.wrong: You can come some time you like.
mistakes.right: You can come any time you like.

points.title: Some 200 people, some idiot, any better, no faster
points.summary: ***Some*** + number = **about** (*some 200 people*). ***Some*** + singular noun = an **unknown** person or thing (*Some idiot parked in my space*). ***Any / no*** + comparative = *at all* (*Is he any better? It's no faster.*).

rows: ***SOME** people think it's a good idea.* (but not everyone)
*Are you feeling **any** better? It isn't **any** easier.*
*The new phone is **no** faster than the old one.*

blocks.md: Use ***no*** or ***none***, not *not any*, at the **start** of a sentence: ***No** students passed. **None** of my friends came.* (not *Not any students passed*)
***Any*** + comparative is common in questions and negatives: *Can't you drive **any** faster?*

examples.text: **Some** man called, but he didn't leave his name.

mistakes.wrong: Not any of the students passed.
The traffic isn't no better today.
mistakes.right: The traffic isn't any better today.

topics.summary: I, you, he, she, it, we, they and my, your, his, her, its, our, their: who does something and who it belongs to.
intro: **Subject pronouns** (*I, you, he, she, it, we, they*) come before the verb: ***She** works in a bank.* **Possessive adjectives** (*my, your, his, her, its, our, their*) come before a noun: ***Her** bank is near **my** house.*
For *me, him, her, us, them*, see [Object Pronouns](/blog/grammar/object-pronouns/). For *mine, yours, hers*, see [Possessive Pronouns](/blog/grammar/possessive-pronouns/).

points.title: Subject pronouns: I, you, he, she, it, we, they
points.summary: Use a **subject pronoun** before the verb: *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*. English sentences **need** a subject: *It's raining.* (not *Is raining*)

rows: *he* (a man / boy), *she* (a woman / girl), *it* (a thing / animal)

blocks.md: English always needs a subject, even when the verb shows who it is in other languages: ***I** am tired.* (not *Am tired*). ***It** is cold today.*
Don't repeat the subject with a pronoun: *My brother lives in Ottawa.* (not *My brother he lives…*)
*I* is always a capital letter.

mistakes.wrong: My father he is a doctor.

points.title: Possessive adjectives: my, your, his, her, its, our, their
points.summary: Use **possessive adjectives** before a noun to show who something belongs to: *my bag, your phone, his car, her house, its tail, our school, their children*.

blocks.md: The possessive adjective agrees with the **owner**, not the thing: *Ali loves **his** mother.* (Ali = he → his). *Sara loves **her** father.* (Sara = she → her).
Possessive adjectives don't change for plural nouns: *my book, my books*.

mistakes.why: the owner is a woman: her

points.title: Its or it's? Their, there or they're? Your or you're?
points.summary: Don't confuse possessive adjectives with short forms: ***its*** (possessive) / ***it's*** (= it is / it has); ***their*** (possessive) / ***there*** (place) / ***they're*** (= they are); ***your*** / ***you're*** (= you are).

blocks.md: Possessive adjectives **never** have an apostrophe: *its, your, their, whose*.
A quick test: can you say *it is, they are, you are, who is*? Then use the apostrophe form.

points.title: It for weather, time and distance; it as an empty subject
points.summary: Use ***it*** as an **empty subject** for weather, time, dates and distance (*It's raining. It's 5 o'clock. It's 10 km to the city.*), before *adjective + to / that* (*It's important to sleep well*), and with ***it takes*** + time.

rows: ***It's** about 5 km from here to the beach.*
***It's** easy to learn. **It's** strange that he didn't call.*
***It takes** an hour to get there.*

blocks.md: English needs a subject even when there's no real “doer”: ***It** is raining* (not *Is raining* or *Rains*).
Put a long *to*-infinitive subject at the end with ***it***: *To learn a language is hard* → ***It's** hard **to learn** a language.* (more natural)

examples.text: How far is **it** to the airport?

mistakes.wrong: This is important to drink water.
It needs two hours to get there.
mistakes.right: It takes two hours to get there.

points.title: Singular they, generic you and one
points.summary: Use ***they / their*** for **one person** when you don't know, or don't want to say, if the person is male or female: *Someone left **their** phone.* Use ***you*** (informal) or ***one*** (very formal) for **people in general**: *You never know.*

rows: *Someone called, but **they** didn't leave a message.*
***You** can't smoke here. **You** never know what will happen.*

blocks.md: Singular ***they*** uses a **plural verb**: *Someone left their bag. **They are** probably looking for it.*
*He or she* is also possible in formal writing, but singular *they* is now standard in most style guides.

examples.text: If a student is late, **they** must sign in at reception.
**You** have to be 18 to vote here.

mistakes.wrong: If a customer complains, they is always right.
mistakes.right: If a customer complains, they are always right.

Ali has a question about his homework, so he's talking to ___ teacher.

I love ___ new phone. I bought it yesterday, and it's great! (one word: a possessive)

topics.summary: Matching the verb to the subject: She works. They work. Everyone is here. One of my friends lives in Paris.
intro: The verb must **agree** with its subject: a **singular** subject takes a **singular** verb (*She **works***), and a **plural** subject takes a **plural** verb (*They **work***).

This is easy with short subjects, but harder with words like *everyone, each* and *one of*, and with long subjects. For group nouns like *team* and *family*, see [Plural Nouns](/blog/grammar/plural-nouns/#pn-group-nouns).

points.title: He works, they work; there is, there are
points.summary: In the present, use **-s** with *he, she, it* and singular nouns (*My brother works*). With *I, you, we, they* and plural nouns, there's no *-s* (*My brothers work*). Use **there is** + singular and **there are** + plural.

blocks.md: ***There is*** + singular or uncountable noun: *There **is** a bank. There **is** some milk.* ***There are*** + plural: *There **are** two banks.*
The past of *be* also changes: *I / he / she / it **was***; *you / we / they **were***. And ***has*** with *he, she, it*: *She **has** a car.*

examples.text: **There is** a park near my house.
**There are** three bedrooms in our flat.

mistakes.wrong: My brother work in a bank.
mistakes.right: My brother works in a bank.

mistakes.wrong: The children is in the garden.
mistakes.right: The children are in the garden.

mistakes.wrong: There is two cafés on my street.
mistakes.right: There are two cafés on my street.

points.title: Everyone is, each student has, one of my friends is
points.summary: ***Everyone, everybody, someone, nobody, everything*** take a **singular** verb (*Everyone is here*). So do ***each*** and ***every*** + noun. ***One of*** + plural noun also takes a **singular** verb (*One of my friends lives in Paris*).

blocks.md: The verb agrees with ***one***, not with the plural noun after *of*: ***One** of the students **is** late.*
After *everyone / someone*, we often use *they / their* to refer back: *Everyone **has** **their** own room.*

examples.text: **One of my friends works** at the airport.

mistakes.wrong: One of my cousins live in Dubai.
mistakes.right: One of my cousins lives in Dubai.

points.title: Long subjects: the list of names is, either… or
points.summary: The verb agrees with the **main noun** of the subject, not the noun closest to it: *The list of names **is** on the wall.* With ***as well as / along with***, it agrees with the **first** subject. With ***either… or / neither… nor***, it agrees with the **nearest** subject.

rows: *The **people** who live next door **are** very kind.*
*as well as, along with, together with*
*The **teacher**, as well as the students, **is** here.*
*Neither my sister nor my **parents are** coming. Either Ali or **Sara is** coming.*
***The number** of students **is** rising. **A number of** students **are** absent.*

blocks.md: Find the **head noun** and ignore *of*-phrases and relative clauses: *The **box** of chocolates **is** on the table.*
***The number of*** = the total (singular verb). ***A number of*** = several (plural verb).

examples.text: The **price** of these shoes **is** too high.
The **students** in my class **come** from ten countries.
Neither the manager nor **the staff were** happy.

mistakes.wrong: The quality of the products are excellent.
mistakes.right: The quality of the products is excellent.

mistakes.wrong: The number of tourists are increasing.
mistakes.right: The number of tourists is increasing.

mistakes.wrong: The manager, as well as his assistants, are coming.
mistakes.right: The manager, as well as his assistants, is coming.

points.title: Amounts, what-clauses and none of them is or are
points.summary: **Amounts** of money, time and distance usually take a **singular** verb (*Ten dollars is enough*). ***What***-clauses usually take a singular verb (*What we need is more time*). With ***none of*** + plural, both singular and plural are used.

rows: ***Two hours is** too long to wait. **Five kilometres is** a long way.*
*None of my friends **has / have** a car.* (singular = more formal)
agrees with the noun: *Most of the **cake is** gone. Most of the **students are** here.*

blocks.md: With ***percentages, fractions*** and ***most / some / all / half of***, the verb agrees with the noun after *of*: *Half of the **money is** gone. Half of the **guests are** here.*

***None of*** + plural: the **singular** verb is traditional and formal; the **plural** is very common and accepted. A ***what***-clause takes a singular verb before a singular complement (*What I need **is** a holiday*); before a plural complement, a plural verb is also common (*What we need **are** new ideas*).

examples.text: **Fifty dollars is** a lot for a T-shirt.
**Most of the information is** out of date.

mistakes.wrong: Fifty kilometres are a long way to drive.
mistakes.right: Fifty kilometres is a long way to drive.

mistakes.wrong: The majority of the work are done.
mistakes.right: The majority of the work is done.

mistakes.wrong: More than one person have called.
mistakes.right: More than one person has called.

topics.summary: Saying that something exists or is in a place: There's a bank near here. There are two bedrooms. Is there any milk?
intro: Use ***there is*** (*there's*) and ***there are*** to say that something **exists** or is **in a place**, especially the **first time** you mention it: ***There's** a café on the corner. **There are** three people in my family.*
For the difference between *there is* and *it is*, see [Introductory It](/blog/grammar/introductory-it/#iit-there-it).

points.title: There's a…, there are some…
points.summary: ***There is / There's*** + **singular** or **uncountable** noun. ***There are*** + **plural** noun: ***There's** a sofa. **There's** some milk. **There are** two chairs.*

rows: ***There are** some books on the table.*
***There are** a lot of people here.*

blocks.md: Don't say *It has* for this meaning: ***There's** a park near my house* (not *It has a park near my house*).

examples.text: **There's** a bank next to the station.
**There are** two cats in the garden.
**There are** lots of good restaurants here.

mistakes.wrong: It has a supermarket near my house.
mistakes.right: There's a supermarket near my house.

points.title: There isn't, there aren't any; Is there…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***There isn't a… / There isn't any…*** (uncountable), ***There aren't any…*** (plural). **Questions**: ***Is there a…? Are there any…?*** Short answers: *Yes, there is. No, there aren't.*

blocks.md: ***There's no*** + noun is another negative form: ***There's no** milk. **There are no** shops.*

examples.text: **There isn't** a cinema in my town.
**Are there** any good cafés near here?

points.title: There was, there were, there will be, there has been
points.summary: Change ***be*** for other tenses: ***there was / were*** (past), ***there will be*** / ***there's going to be*** (future), ***there has / have been*** (present perfect).

blocks.md: In questions, put the verb or auxiliary before ***there***: ***Was there** a problem? **Will there be** food? **Has there been** any news?*

examples.text: **There was** a lot of traffic this morning.
**There will be** a test next week.
**There has been** an accident on the highway.

mistakes.wrong: There was many people at the concert.
mistakes.right: There were many people at the concert.

mistakes.wrong: There will have a party on Saturday.
mistakes.right: There will be a party on Saturday.

points.title: There must be, there seems to be, there used to be
points.summary: ***There*** works with **modals** and other verbs: ***there must / might / could / should be***, ***there seems / appears to be***, ***there used to be***, ***there's bound / likely to be***.

rows: ***There should be** more buses at night.*
***There used to be** a cinema here.*

blocks.md: In informal speech, people often say ***there's*** + plural: *There's two problems.* In writing, use ***there are***.

examples.text: **There seems to be** something wrong with my phone.
**There used to be** a park here.

mistakes.right: There seems to be a problem.

mistakes.wrong: It used to be a cinema here. (it existed)
mistakes.right: There used to be a cinema here.

points.title: There's no point in, there's no need to, for there to be
points.summary: Fixed patterns: ***There's no point (in)*** + *-ing*, ***There's no need to*** + verb, ***There's no way*** + clause, ***There's nothing like…***, ***for there to be***, and formal ***there is said / thought to be***.

rows: ***There's no way** I'm paying that much.*
*It's unusual **for there to be** snow in April.*
***There is said to be** gold in the hills.*

blocks.md: After ***there's no point (in)***, use ***-ing***: *There's no point **complaining*** (not *to complain*).

examples.text: **There's no point in** arguing. He won't change his mind.
**There's no need to** book. Just come.
We don't want **there to be** any problems.

mistakes.wrong: There's no point to wait any longer.
mistakes.right: There's no point (in) waiting any longer.

mistakes.wrong: There's no need that you come.
mistakes.right: There's no need for you to come.

topics.summary: Pointing to things near and far: this book, that house, these shoes, those people.
intro: Use ***this*** (singular) and ***these*** (plural) for things **near** you, and ***that*** (singular) and ***those*** (plural) for things **far** from you: ***This** is my bag. **That** car over there is my dad's.*
They're also used for time (*this week, in those days*), in conversation (*That's great!*) and in writing to refer back to ideas (*This means that…*).

points.title: This, that, these, those: near and far
points.summary: ***This*** + singular and ***these*** + plural = **near**. ***That*** + singular and ***those*** + plural = **far**.

blocks.md: Use them **before a noun** (*this phone*) or **alone** (*What's **this**?*).
The verb agrees: ***This is**… / **These are**…* and ***That is**… / **Those are**…*

points.title: This is…, that's great, this one
points.summary: Use ***this*** to introduce people (*This is my friend*) and on the phone (*Hi, this is Sara*). ***That's*** reacts to what someone has just said (*That's great!*). ***This one / that one*** replace a noun.

rows: *I passed! ~ **That's** great! That's a good idea.*

blocks.md: *That* often refers to something **just said**: *I'm getting married. ~ Really? **That's** wonderful!*
*This one / that one* avoid repeating the noun: *Which cake do you want? ~ **That one**, please.* With plurals, *these / those* alone is more common than *these ones*.

examples.text: Hi, **this is** Sara. Can I speak to Leila?
I've found a new job. ~ **That's** fantastic!

mistakes.wrong: Hello, I am Sara speaking. (on the phone)

points.title: This morning, that day, these days, in those days
points.summary: ***This*** + time = the **present** or a **near** time (*this morning, this week*). ***That*** + time = a **past** time we've mentioned (*that day, that night*). ***These days*** = nowadays; ***in those days*** = at that time in the past.

rows: the morning of today / the current week / year
a time in the past that we've mentioned
at that time in the past

blocks.md: When telling a story, use ***that***: *We met in 2015. **That** summer was amazing.*
In reported speech, *this* often changes to *that*: *“I'm busy this week.” → She said she was busy **that** week.* See [Reported Speech](/blog/grammar/reported-speech/).

examples.text: **In those days**, there was no internet.

mistakes.wrong: I didn't sleep well this night. (meaning last night)
mistakes.right: I didn't sleep well last night.

mistakes.wrong: In these days, people worked longer hours. (in the past)
mistakes.right: In those days, people worked longer hours.

points.title: This and that in writing: this means, those who
points.summary: In writing, ***this*** often refers to an idea **just mentioned** (*This means that…*). ***That*** refers to what another person said. ***Those who*** = the people who; ***that of / those of*** replace a noun (*higher than those of last year*).

rows: *A: Let's leave early. B: **That**'s a good idea.*
***Those who** arrived late missed the talk.*
*Our prices are lower than **those of** our competitors.*

blocks.md: In formal writing, ***this*** + a summary noun is clearer than *this* alone: *this **situation**, this **change**, this **approach***.
***That of / those of*** replace a noun to avoid repeating it: *The climate of Vancouver is milder than **that of** Toronto.* (= the climate of) Use *those of* for plurals.

examples.text: Sleep improves memory. **This** is why students should rest before exams.
**Those who** want to join should sign up today.
The climate here is warmer than **that of** northern Europe.

mistakes.wrong: Them who arrived late missed the start.
mistakes.right: Those who arrived late missed the start.

mistakes.wrong: Our results are better than these of last year.
mistakes.right: Our results are better than those of last year.

mistakes.wrong: The population of Toronto is bigger than Montreal.
mistakes.right: The population of Toronto is bigger than that of Montreal.
mistakes.why: compare the same things: that of

points.title: Storytelling this, shared that, and not that hungry
points.summary: In informal stories, ***this*** introduces something **new** (*So this man comes up to me…*). ***That*** refers to **shared memories** or shows dislike (*Remember that café? I hate that noise.*). ***That*** + adjective = *very / so* (*I'm not that hungry*).

rows: *There was **this** strange guy on the bus…* (like *a*, but more vivid)
*I'm not **that** hungry. I didn't know it was **that** expensive.*

blocks.md: ***That*** + adjective (informal) means *so* or *very*: *The film wasn't **that** good.* (= not very good)
***It*** simply refers back to something already mentioned. ***This*** draws attention or points forward to new information: *Here's the plan. **This** is what we'll do.*

examples.text: So I'm in a shop, and **this** woman starts shouting at me.
Remember **that** little restaurant near the beach?
Listen to **this**: I've got the job!

topics.h1: The Verb To Be (Am, Is, Are)
topics.summary: The most important verb in English: I am, you are, he is. Forms, negatives, questions, and common mistakes.
intro: ***Be*** is the most common verb in English. In the present, it has three forms: ***am, is, are***: *I **am** a student. She **is** from Iran. We **are** happy.* In the past: ***was, were***.
This page covers the present forms and uses of *be*. For the past, see [Was and Were](/blog/grammar/was-were/).

points.title: I am, you are, he is: forms and contractions
points.summary: ***I am*** (I'm), ***you / we / they are*** ('re), ***he / she / it is*** ('s). In speaking, we usually use the **short forms**.

blocks.md: With a **noun** subject, use *is* (singular) or *are* (plural): *My brother **is** a doctor. My parents **are** teachers.*
Don't confuse ***it's*** (= it is) and ***its*** (possessive): ***It's** a nice car. **Its** colour is red.*

points.title: I'm not, isn't, aren't; Are you…?
points.summary: **Negative**: ***I'm not, he isn't (is not), they aren't (are not)***. **Questions**: put *be* first: ***Are** you OK? **Is** she here?* Short answers: *Yes, I am. No, she isn't.*

blocks.md: Say ***I'm not*** (not *I amn't*). Both ***he isn't*** and ***he's not*** are correct.
In positive short answers, don't use contractions: *Yes, I **am**.* (not *Yes, I'm.*)

examples.text: **Are** you from Spain? ~ No, I'**m not**.

points.title: I'm 25, I'm hungry, I'm cold: be, not have
points.summary: English uses ***be*** (not *have*) for **age** (*I'm 25*), **feelings** (*I'm hungry, I'm cold, I'm afraid*), **jobs** (*She's a doctor*), **nationality**, and **be born** (*I was born in 1990*).

rows: *I born in Shiraz. / I am born in Shiraz.*

blocks.md: ***Be born*** is in the **past** for when you came into the world: *I **was born** in 1995.*

examples.text: Are you **cold**? I can close the window.

mistakes.wrong: I have cold. Close the window.

points.title: I agree, not I'm agree: be or do?
points.summary: Don't use ***be*** with other verbs in the present simple: *I **agree*** (not *I'm agree*), *I **don't understand*** (not *I'm not understand*), ***Do** you like…?* (not *Are you like…?*). Use ***be*** with **adjectives**, **nouns** and **-ing**.

blocks.md: Ask yourself: is there **another verb**? Then use ***do / does*** for questions and negatives: *Do you **live** here?* Is there **no other verb** (just an adjective or noun)? Then use ***be***: *Are you **tired**?*

points.title: He's being silly: be in the continuous
points.summary: ***Be*** can be continuous (***am / is / are being***) to talk about **temporary behaviour**: *You're **being** very rude today.* (= you're acting rudely now). It's also used in the **passive continuous**: *The road **is being** repaired.*

blocks.md: Use ***being*** + adjective for **actions and behaviour**: *silly, rude, kind, careful, lazy, stupid, difficult, nice*. Not for states like *tall* or *tired*: *He's tired* (not *He's being tired*).

examples.text: She's usually shy, but today she's **being** very friendly.
My car **is being** fixed this week.

topics.summary: The past of be: I was tired, they were at home, Were you there?
intro: *Was* and *were* are the past forms of *be* (*am / is / are*): *I **was** at home yesterday. They **were** late.*
They are some of the most common words in English. This page starts with the basic forms and goes on to the mistakes learners often make with *did*, and to *were* in *If I were you*.

points.title: I was, you were: the forms
points.summary: I / he / she / it **was**; you / we / they **were**.

blocks.md: Use *was / were* with past time words: *yesterday, last night, last week, two days ago, in 2015, when I was a child*.

There are only two forms. **Was** goes with *I, he, she, it* and singular nouns (*my brother was*). **Were** goes with *you, we, they* and plural nouns (*my parents were*). *You* is always **were**, even for one person.

examples.text: My parents **were** in Spain last month.

examples.note: you → were, even for one person

points.title: Wasn't, weren't and questions
points.summary: Negative: **wasn't / weren't**. Questions: **Was** he…? **Were** you…? No *did*.

blocks.md: For questions, put *was / were* **before** the subject: *She was tired.* → ***Was** she tired?* With a question word: ***Where were** you? **Why was** he angry? **How was** your weekend?*
Don't use *did* with *was / were*. Not *Did you were at home?* but ***Were** you at home?*

examples.text: **Were** you at the meeting? ~ No, I **wasn't**.

points.title: Was born, was / were + adjective, it was
points.summary: *I **was born** in 1995.* (not *I born*). Use *was / were* to describe the past: *It was cold. They were nervous.*

blocks.md: To say when or where someone started life, use ***was / were born***: *I **was born** in Tehran. My twins **were born** in May.* Not *I born* or *I am born*.
Use *was / were* + adjective or noun to describe things in the past: *The food **was** delicious. The people **were** friendly. My first car **was** a Fiat.*
Use ***it was*** for the weather, time and opinions: ***It was** sunny. **It was** 10 o'clock. **It was** a great day.*
For something that exists in the past, use ***there was / there were***: ***There was** a problem. **There were** a lot of people.* See [There Is and There Are](/blog/grammar/there-is-there-are/).

points.title: Was / were or did?
points.summary: *Was / were* + adjective, noun, place or *-ing*. *Did* + base verb. Don't mix them.

blocks.md: Use *was / were* when the main word is an adjective (*tired*), a noun (*a doctor*) or a place (*at home*). Use *did / didn't* with a **verb** (*go, like, see*).

Positive sentences with other verbs don't need *was / were*: *I **went** home.* Not *I was go home*. (*Was* + *-ing* is the past continuous: *I **was going** home.* See [Past Continuous](/blog/grammar/past-continuous/).)

examples.text: I **was** hungry, so I **made** a sandwich.
**Were** you at the gym? ~ No, I **didn't go** today.
The film **wasn't** bad, but I **didn't love** it.
**Did** they **enjoy** the trip? ~ Yes, it **was** fantastic.

mistakes.wrong: I was go to the park.

points.title: Were after if and wish: If I were you…
points.summary: In unreal sentences we often use **were** for all persons: *If I **were** you… I wish it **were** Friday.*

blocks.md: In sentences about **unreal** or imaginary situations, we can use ***were*** with *I, he, she, it*: *If I **were** rich, I'd travel the world. I wish she **were** here.*
In everyday speech, *was* is also common here: *If I **was** rich…* Both are correct. ***Were*** is more formal and is the usual choice in writing.
In the fixed phrase for advice, always use ***were***: ***If I were you**, I'd take the job.* (*If I was you* is very informal.)
This *were* is not about the past. It is about now or an imagined situation. See [Second Conditional](/blog/grammar/second-conditional/) and [Wish and If Only](/blog/grammar/wish-if-only/).

examples.text: **If I were you**, I'd call her.
If he **were** taller, he could play basketball.
She talks as if she **were** the boss.

mistakes.wrong: If I am you, I would apologise.
mistakes.right: If I were you, I would apologise.

topics.summary: How English sentences are built: subject + verb + object, then place, then time. I bought a coat in town yesterday.
intro: English word order is quite **fixed**: ***subject + verb + object***: *Sara **loves** coffee.* (not *Sara coffee loves*). Information about **place** and **time** usually comes at the end, in that order.
This page shows the basic order, where adverbs go, and how to use two objects.

points.title: Subject + verb + object
points.summary: The normal order is **subject + verb + object** (*I like tea*). Don't put anything **between** the verb and its object: *I like tea very much* (not *I like very much tea*).

blocks.md: In English the **subject** comes before the verb in statements, even with the weather: ***It*** *is raining.*
Keep the verb and its object **together**: *She speaks English well.* (not *She speaks well English*)

points.title: Place before time: at the station yesterday
points.summary: At the end of a sentence, put **place** before **time**: *I met her **at the station yesterday**.* With manner too, the usual order is **manner → place → time**: *She worked **hard at the office all day**.*

blocks.md: **Time** expressions can also go at the **start**: ***Yesterday** I met Ali at the station.*
Words like *today* and *tomorrow* go at the end or the start, not in the middle: *I'm working **today**.* (not *I'm today working*)

examples.text: I bought this jacket **in Toronto last year**.
She goes **to the gym every morning**.
**Last night** we ate **at a Persian restaurant**.

mistakes.wrong: We arrived last night in Paris.
mistakes.right: We arrived in Paris last night.

points.title: Where do adverbs go? Also, probably, already, only
points.summary: Many short adverbs go in the **middle** of the sentence: **before the main verb**, but **after** *be* and the first **auxiliary**: *I **also** like tea. She's **probably** at home. We've **already** eaten.*

rows: *also, just, already, still, probably, definitely, even, only, almost*

blocks.md: With negatives, *probably* and *definitely* come **before** the negative auxiliary: *I **probably won't** be late.* Most other adverbs come after it: *I **don't often** go.*
***Only*** goes before the word it describes, and this can change the meaning: ***Only** I saw her* (nobody else) / *I **only** saw her* (I didn't speak to her).

mistakes.wrong: They have finished already their homework.
mistakes.right: They have already finished their homework.
mistakes.why: not between the verb and its object

points.title: Two objects: give me the book, give the book to me
points.summary: Verbs like ***give, send, show, lend, tell*** can have two objects: ***give** someone something* (*She gave me a present*) or ***give** something **to** someone* (*She gave a present to me*). With *buy, make, get, cook*, use ***for***.

rows: verb + thing + *for* + person (*buy, make, get, cook*)
*Give **it** to me.* (*Give me it* is informal)

blocks.md: When the thing is a **pronoun** (*it, them*), use *to / for*: *Can you send **it to** me?*
Some verbs only take ***to*** + person: ***explain** it **to** me, **describe** it **to** her, **say** something **to** him* (not *explain me it*).

examples.text: Can you lend **your car** **to my brother**?

mistakes.wrong: Can you explain me the problem?
mistakes.right: Can you explain the problem to me?

mistakes.wrong: She bought a present to her mother.
mistakes.right: She bought a present for her mother.

points.title: Fronting for emphasis and here comes the bus
points.summary: For **emphasis** or **contrast**, English sometimes puts an object or phrase at the **start** (*That film I'll never forget*). After *here / there* and place phrases at the start, the verb can come **before** a noun subject (*Here comes the bus. On the hill stood an old castle.*).

rows: ***Here comes** the bus! **There goes** my money.* (but: *Here **it comes**.*)
***On the hill stood** an old castle.*
***Strange as it may seem**, I enjoyed it.*

blocks.md: With **pronouns**, don't invert after *here / there*: *Here **it** comes* (not *Here comes it*). *There **she** is!*
Fronting is common in speech for contrast and in literary writing for effect. For *Never have I…*, see [Inversion After Negative Adverbials](/blog/grammar/inversion-negative-adverbials/).

examples.text: **In the corner sat** an old man.
**Tired as she was**, she kept working.

mistakes.wrong: Tired as was she, she kept going.
mistakes.right: Tired as she was, she kept going.
