topics.h1: Would Like, Would Rather and Prefer
topics.summary: Saying what you want and prefer, politely: I'd like a coffee. I'd rather stay in. I prefer tea to coffee.
intro: ***Would like*** is a polite way to say *want*: *I**'d like** a glass of water, please.* ***Would rather*** and ***prefer*** say which of two things you want more: *I**'d rather** walk. I **prefer** tea to coffee.*

These phrases are everywhere in daily English: ordering food, making plans and being polite. For *would rather* + another person (*I'd rather you didn't*), see [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/#up-would-rather).

points.title: I'd like…, Would you like…?
points.summary: **would like** + noun or **to + verb** = a polite *want*: *I'd like a tea. I'd like to go home.* **Would you like…?** offers and invites.

rows: ***Would you like to** come with us?*
*Yes, please. / No, thank you. / Yes, I'd love to.*

blocks.md: ***I'd*** = *I would*. *Would like* is more polite than *want*, especially when you ask for something: *I**'d like** the chicken, please* (better than *I want the chicken*).
Use ***to*** + verb after *would like*: *I'd like **to** see the menu.* Not *I'd like see* or *I'd like seeing*.

examples.text: **Would** you **like** something to eat? ~ Yes, please.
**Would** you **like to** dance? ~ I**'d love to**!

mistakes.right: I'd like to see the doctor.

mistakes.wrong: Would you like to a coffee?

points.title: Like or would like?
points.summary: **like** = enjoy, in general: *I like swimming.* **would like** = want, now or on one occasion: *I'd like to swim now.*

rows: *I**'d like** a coffee.* (I want one now.)

blocks.md: ***Like*** is usually followed by *-ing* (or *to* + verb): *I **like reading** / **to read**.*
***Would like*** is followed by ***to*** + verb, never *-ing*: *I'd like **to read** that book.*
In questions, the difference is important: ***Do you like** tea?* asks about your taste. ***Would you like** tea?* is an offer.

mistakes.wrong: Do you like a drink? (an offer)
I'd like going to the concert.
mistakes.right: I'd like to go to the concert.

points.title: I'd rather…: what you prefer
points.summary: **would rather + base verb** = would prefer: *I'd rather stay at home.* **would rather … than** compares two things: *I'd rather walk than take the bus.*

blocks.md: ***I'd rather*** (*I would rather*) + **base verb** (no *to*) says what we prefer in a particular situation: *Are you hungry? ~ No, I**'d rather** just **have** a drink.*
To compare: ***would rather*** + verb ***than*** + verb: *I**'d rather** read **than** watch TV.*
Negative: ***would rather not*** + base verb: *I**'d rather not** talk about it.*
Questions: ***Would you rather** have tea or coffee?*
When you want **another person** to do something, the pattern changes to the past: *I'd rather **you stayed**.* See [Unreal Past](/blog/grammar/unreal-past/#up-would-rather).

examples.text: She**'d rather** stay in **than** go to the party.
**Would** you **rather** live in the city or the countryside?

mistakes.wrong: I'd rather walk than taking a taxi.
mistakes.right: I'd rather walk than take a taxi.

points.title: Prefer and would prefer
points.summary: **prefer** (in general): *I prefer tea **to** coffee. I prefer walking **to** driving.* **would prefer** (now): *I'd prefer **to** walk (**rather than** drive).*

rows: *I**'d prefer to** stay in tonight (**rather than** go out).*

blocks.md: ***Prefer*** is for preferences **in general**. ***Would prefer*** is for a **particular** situation, like *would rather*: *I**'d prefer to** eat now.* = *I**'d rather** eat now.*
After *prefer … to*, use **to** as a preposition (*to driving*), not *than*: *I prefer cats **to** dogs.* Not *I prefer cats than dogs*.

examples.text: I **prefer** working at home **to** working in an office.
I**'d prefer to** sit by the window, please.
She**'d prefer to** take a taxi **rather than** wait for the bus.

mistakes.right: I'd prefer to stay at home.

points.title: I'd like you to…, I'd prefer you to…, I'd prefer it if…
points.summary: To talk about what you want **someone else** to do: **would like / would prefer + person + to + verb**, or **would prefer it if + past**: *I'd like you to call me.*

rows: *I**'d like you to** meet my parents.*
*would prefer it if* + person + past simple

blocks.md: Don't use a *that* clause after *would like*: *I'd like **you to** come.* Not *I'd like that you come*.
*Would prefer it if* and *would rather* + past simple are very polite ways to ask someone not to do something.

examples.text: I**'d like you to** finish this by Friday.
examples.note: what I want you to do

examples.text: My parents **would like me to** study medicine.
I**'d prefer you not to** mention it.
I**'d prefer it if** you **called** before visiting.

mistakes.wrong: I'd like that you help me.
mistakes.right: I'd like you to help me.

mistakes.wrong: I'd prefer it if you don't tell anyone.
mistakes.right: I'd prefer it if you didn't tell anyone.

points.title: I would have liked to…, I'd rather have…
points.summary: For past wishes that didn't happen: **would have liked to + verb** (or *would like to have done*), **would rather have + past participle**, **would have preferred to**.

blocks.md: To say you wanted something in the past but it **didn't happen**, use:

items: ***would have liked to*** + base verb: *I **would have liked to** see the museum, but there wasn't time.*
***would like to have*** + past participle (same meaning, a little more formal): *I **would like to have** met her.*
***would have preferred to*** + base verb: *She **would have preferred to** stay in a hotel.*
***would rather have*** + past participle: *I**'d rather have** gone by train.* (We didn't.)

blocks.md: Don't put *have* in both places. *I would have liked to **see** it* is better than *I would have liked to have seen it* (which is common in speech but criticised in careful writing).

examples.text: I **would have liked to** say goodbye.
We**'d have preferred to** sit outside, but it was raining.
I**'d rather have** stayed at home. The party was boring.
She **would like to have** studied art.

mistakes.wrong: I would have like to come.
mistakes.right: I would have liked to come.
